#3268. Meet the 20 first-place apps from RevenueCat’s Shipaton 2026

A cozy habit tracker, a smarter snippet library, and a rooster that wants you out of bed: this year’s Shipaton winners offer plenty of new apps to explore.

RevenueCat’s annual app-building competition drew 3,985 project submissions in 2026, according to its winner announcement. Across the 20 first-place categories, developers tackled everyday frustrations, built inventive games, and found new ways to connect people.

You can get a look at every first place winner below, and read RevenueCat’s full winner announcement for every more.

Keeping a routine is easier when there’s something to look forward to. Mio pairs self-care and habit tracking with a pixel companion that grows as you make progress. Check off habits, earn coins, and unlock new companions and collectibles, with friends and groups adding a social reason to keep going.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

That dog you met on your morning walk can become part of your collection. Boop identifies cats and dogs and turns their photos into stickers for a digital book, giving pet lovers a playful reason to pay attention to the animals around them.

Creator Taiwo Omisore’s “100 Boops” challenge took the app into the real world, where printed pet portraits and conversations with owners helped shape the product. That hands-on approach earned Boop first place in #BuildInPublic.

If you have fond memories of futuristic arcade racers, Nitelore has a familiar appeal: hovering vehicles, neon tracks, and plenty of speed. Chase your own ghost in time trials, take on combat races, or compete online.

Free tracks offer a starting point, while paid unlocks and daily and weekly challenges give players more to explore. RevenueCat’s Best Game judges singled out the art direction, effects, and haptics.

Explaining how you see color can be surprisingly difficult. See as Me: Colorblind makes that conversation visual, using a split-screen camera to compare different types and degrees of color blindness. A shareable link lets someone else see the comparison without installing the app.

Developer Javier Jiménez drew on his own experience with protanopia. That personal perspective helped the app earn the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Its personality runs through the entire interface, including a time picker that uses the rooster’s scrolling eyes and yellow beak. That consistent character, animation, and attention to detail earned Clucky the RevenueCat Design Award.

Adversary starts with a familiar challenge: flip cards and find matching pairs. The catch is a hidden Danger card with no matching partner. Reveal it, and an ad becomes part of the board you’re trying to remember.

That idea earned Niv Ben-porath’s game the Catvertising Award. Players can continue with ads after an initial ad-free period, or choose a permanent unlock that removes ads and adds difficulty options.

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Built by four software engineering students at Université Laval, the Next Gen Award winner uses the phones people already have to create a shared activity. Its Shipaton submission includes ten minigames. The winner announcement links to the Android release on Google Play.

1st place • HAMM Award (Help Apps Make Money)

GRIDLOCK takes a game everyone knows and adds up to four players, online rooms, and eleven special moves. The result offers more ways to disrupt an opponent’s plans than the familiar three-by-three board.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

1st place • Influencer Award – Nutrition & Healthy Eating: Abbey’s Kitchen

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

1st place • Influencer Award – Productivity: Christopher Lawley

The reply you send every week, the PDF you keep hunting for, and the image you paste repeatedly can all live in SnipStash. It organizes reusable text, images, and files across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with a keyboard, Mac quick palette, hotkeys, and Shortcuts bringing them within reach.

Private iCloud sync connects the library across devices. Its speed and native interface helped it win Christopher Lawley’s productivity challenge.

1st place • Influencer Award – Career Coaching: Leadership Heather

Knowing what you want to say and saying it aloud are different things. Rehearse – Hard Conversations gives you an AI counterpart to practice with before a difficult workplace discussion.

Choose from 33 prepared scenarios or bring your own situation, then review feedback on clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and structure. A prep card helps you take the useful points into the real conversation. The app won Leadership Heather’s career-coaching challenge for its focused, straightforward approach.

1st place • Influencer Award – Gaming: Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming

You see a game in a short video, mean to look it up later, and forget its name. Game Magnet lets you share the clip to identify the games and save them to your backlog.

Processing happens in the background, with a notification when the result is ready. Shelves, ratings, and ranked lists help organize what comes next. The app won Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming’s challenge by making discovery and keeping track of games easier.

1st place • Influencer Award – Yoga & Fitness: Simone Sharice

FeelGood: Movement Menu starts with a short check-in about your energy, available time, and how you want to feel. It then offers a small menu of movement, with an appetizer, main, and optional sides.

The options span yoga, Pilates, strength, walking, stretching, and breathing. Rest is part of the experience, too. Yusra Salam and Ameena Malik’s app won Simone Sharice’s yoga and fitness challenge, with judges praising its calm, inviting design.

BoatBrawl brings arcade boat battles to a group of up to eight players. Steer, fire, and scramble through interactive arenas, with bots and shared-screen play offering more ways to join in.

Rehaan Cubes and Ashwin K M used Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to bring the game across phones and computers, including iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, and the web. Its smooth browser play helped it take JetBrains’ Ship Kotlin Everywhere award.

Trazo: Golf Ball Tracer adds a ball-flight line to your own golf videos. Select the ball twice to start, and the processing runs on the phone.

Julian Praest’s app won Most Viral App for the way its team introduced the product through organic content. Golf humor and practical advice set up the tracer reveal, making the finished video part of the pitch. For golfers, the appeal is simple: make the shot easier to follow when you share it.

One Piece Card Game collectors know that similar-looking cards can be very different finds. Grandfolio helps identify artwork variants, manage duplicates, and track collection prices and progress.

The Best App for Galaxy winner impressed judges with layouts that adapt to folded, tabletop, and open-screen use. There’s an App Store release for Apple users, too, making this a relevant discovery even if your collection starts on an iPhone.

Let’s Get Support by 3Dadz is designed for partners, parents, and friends affected by someone else’s addiction. Check-ins, journaling, boundary-setting tools, and local resources give those supporters a place to focus on their own needs.

Joshua Burgess and Aaryn B. built the app from community conversations in British Columbia, using Replit to turn the idea into a live product. It won Replit’s Idea to Income award. The announcement links to its Android release.

PoquitoTalk: Bocas del Toro turns English into local Spanish voice notes for WhatsApp and helps translate the replies. The recipient doesn’t need to install the app, keeping the conversation in a tool people already use.

Creator Dorien Van den Abbeele drew on years of life in Bocas del Toro. Its Growth Loop Award recognizes extensive growth experiments and an honest account of what the measurements could show. The announcement links to Google Play.

Parky! combines wait times, dining availability, and memories from Disney and Universal visits. Built by former Disney Cast Member Chase Van Derrick, it aims to offer useful help throughout a park day.

Dining alerts can become conversations on the Lock Screen, where you can ask about another time or restaurant. Alongside queue Live Activities and recap messages, those interactive notifications helped Parky! win the Keep Them Coming Back Award.

In Your Own Words offers short, real-world speaking scenarios and feedback on pace, hesitation, and filler words. Speech analysis takes place on the phone, giving users a way to practice the words before they need them.

Natasha Wilson’s app won the Funnel Vision Award for connecting a web quiz, a relevant practice deck, and a web purchase that unlocks access in the app. The introduction to the product begins before the download.

Friendpire turns the idea of a board-game night with friends into a shared hex-tile world. Gather resources, build farms and docks, and grow an empire together. RevenueCat employee Erik MacInnis built the game to make it easier to stay connected with friends who rarely find time to play.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

#3267. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3266. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign gets new update from leaker

Apple reportedly has a big redesign coming to next year’s iPhone Pro models, timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. The latest leak about the design reveals that the dream of a cutout-free display may remain a dream for now.

Yesterday Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station outlined three new iPhone models coming in early 2027: iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, and iPhone Air 2.

His main focus was on the iPhone 18, which is expected to get two Pro-inspired upgrades.

In a follow-up post though, replying to another Weibo user’s question, the leaker addressed a key design question regarding next fall’s iPhone Pro models.

Apple is rumored to be working on a big redesign timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. It will reportedly feature a quad-curved display that wraps around the edges of the device for a visually bezel-free look.

Early rumors indicated the device could also drop the Dynamic Island for a truly all-glass display, with no cutouts.

The Duo2 will also have faceID and will steal the show. Who wants curved glass on all sides of the phone? We all remember how that went for Galaxy Edge phones.

But according to Digital Chat Station, that’s not happening after all.

After being asked if the ‘iPhone 20 Pro Max’ will have a Dynamic Island still, or feature a hole-free display, the leaker confirmed the display will still have holes. Thus, it will retain the Dynamic Island cutout.

It’s unclear if the Dynamic Island will be the same size as that of iPhone 18 Pro, but since the device is expected to have Face ID, that’s highly likely.

Does the inclusion of a display cutout change your interest in the iPhone 20 Pro at all? Let us know in the comments.

#3264. Report: Apple reduces employees’ AI token allowances as Ternus moves to cut costs

Bloomberg reports that Apple has begun reducing employees’ daily AI spending limits, with some engineers seeing their allowances cut from $300 to $200, and further reductions planned across multiple teams. Here are the details.

Over the past year, tokenmaxxing, the practice of consuming as many AI tokens as possible, often as a measure of productivity, took over Silicon Valley, with companies such as Meta even introducing internal leaderboards, some unofficial, ranking employees by their AI token usage.

Tokenmaxxing emerged alongside improvements in AI agents’ coding capabilities, as tools such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor became increasingly popular among software developers.

Unsurprisingly, companies soon began to rein in token usage as the rising costs of AI tools raised questions about whether the productivity gains justified the expense. Just recently, Accenture reportedly reduced its centrally funded Claude allowance to just $29 per employee per month, requiring any additional spending to be covered by individual projects or teams.

And while there hadn’t been reports of disproportionate token usage from engineers and other employees at Apple, Bloomberg reported today that the company is also looking to rein in employees’ AI spending as part of CEO John Ternus’ broader cost-cutting efforts.

Last month, Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap for some engineers using AI models to $200 from $300, according to people with knowledge of the change. The company is now planning further cuts for some engineering teams, potentially reducing their daily allowances to as little as $100, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

Many groups outside of engineering already face a $100 daily cap, but Apple has considered reducing that limit to as little as $25 for some teams, the people said. Employees who require higher allowances to perform their jobs will be able to seek exemptions from senior leadership.

It is not immediately clear which tools are affected by the new spending limits. However, Bloomberg reports that Apple employees have access to several AI services, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Google’s Gemini. Some teams are also being encouraged to use cheaper AI models or models that run locally on their devices to reduce costs.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman had previously said that Apple was heavily reliant on Anthropic’s AI models for its internal operations, describing the company as essentially “running on Anthropic,” despite its partnership with Google to power Siri.

That came a few months after then-CEO Tim Cook encouraged employees to make greater use of AI in their daily work during an all-hands meeting, saying, “All of us are using AI in a significant way already, and we must use it as a company as well.”

$200-$300 per day is a pretty high amount. There are certainly people and tasks that can effectively put that many tokens to efficient use, but my guess is that most people bumping those limits could be more efficient in their use.

You’re going to always have that one person who complains about the budget but is out there making small code changes running Fable on max. These blanket token budgets typically seek to limit damage from those types while those that can make a case for why they need more budget typically get it.

Back to today’s report, Bloomberg says employee reactions to the new spending limits have been mixed. According to its sources, “few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances,” while others “see the reductions as a sign of broader cost cutting, adding to concerns about potential layoffs.”

Interestingly, the cuts come as Apple’s overall spending continues to rise. Earlier this week, Apple reported its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings, bringing its fiscal year to a close with R&D expenses up 32% to $45.8 billion, driven in part by higher infrastructure and AI costs.

Bloomberg notes that it remains unclear how much Apple will actually save through the new restrictions, particularly since some employees weren’t using their full allowances to begin with.

When Apple announced the new MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR display, I started feeling nervous about the battery life.

In this new era of notebooks, the Cupertino crew has crammed a massive power-hungry OLED touchscreen into an even thinner chassis, and built a backlight for that Apple logo on the lid for good measure. Historically, you can’t do these and keep the battery life worry-free.

Well, after walking out of the testing lab, I have to admit I was wrong. The PROLED MacBook Pro doesn’t just match the endurance of its bulkier mini-LED predecessors — it rolls and smokes the entire Windows AI PC ecosystem in the process.

Let’s look at the raw data. The 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display (M5 Max) clocked in at an absurd 21 hours and 24 minutes on our continuous web-surfing battery test.

That isn’t just good; it effectively ties to the thicker, non-touch 16-inch mini-LED M5 Pro model. Meanwhile, the 14-inch PROLED with M5 Pro pushed out an incredibly respectable time at just shy of 17 hours. It’s within striking distance of the 14-inch mini-LED with M5 Max, but there’s definitely a gap (17:58).

Apple managed to integrate a drastically superior, brighter, touch-sensitive OLED panel, a glowing logo and thin out the chassis without triggering a battery life collapse.

But the real story here is the absolute bloodbath happening on the Windows side of the aisle.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Over the past few months, I’ve been following Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops closely — testing one myself over the past month. Alongside that, I’ve been close to the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme too, with both of these heavily touted as definitive “MacBook killers.”

And while I can point to some stats that do show these as worthy competitors, if endurance is the battleground that matters to you, they never even showed up to the fight.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra running RTX Spark dies at 10 hours and 35 minutes. The Lenovo Yoga 9n (also Spark) tapped out three minutes earlier. Even the Asus Zenbook A16 with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme collapsed at 10 hours and 26 minutes.

You could literally charge your 16-inch PROLED to 100%, browse the web for an entire day, let these laptops start fully charged right next to it, and the MacBook will still outlast it.

I criticize Apple for its exorbitant pricing — especially when it comes to the PROLED. But when it comes to performance and power efficiency gains, the conversation is over.

The Windows ecosystem is feeling the weight of local AI power demands, while Apple just casually dropped an impossibly thin, touchscreen OLED flagship that runs for nearly a full 24 hours.

This AI PC revolution might be taking off, but when it comes to keeping the lights on, the rest of the industry isn’t just losing to Apple — they aren’t even playing the same sport.

#3262. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

Tobi will start by discussing business highlights from our third quarter. Sonia will discuss our financial results in greater detail along with our outlook. We will finish the call with Q&A. Before I turn the call over to Tobi, I would like to draw your attention to our forward-looking statements and the description and definition of non-GAAP financial measures, which can be found in our presentation. We will be discussing certain non-GAAP financial measures, including adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin, adjusted operating expenses, adjusted net income, and free cash flow.

Reconciliations of these non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in the financial tables included with our earnings press release and in the appendix of our presentation. Any forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties. For more information, please refer to the risk factors included in our SEC filings, including those in our most recently filed 10-K, which is available on the IR section of our website. We assume no obligation to update any forward-looking statements. Now I will turn the call over to Tobi.

Tobi Hartmann: Thank you, Katherine, and thanks to those joining us to review third quarter 2026 results. We delivered another quarter of steady execution against our financial and strategic goals. Q3 revenue of $182 million was within our guidance range and up slightly year-over-year. Marketplace, where we have been continually improving value delivery and winning customers, grew revenue by 5% year-over-year. In keeping with our focus on development velocity, we launched our first self-service marketplace offering to better attract and serve the smaller independent dealer segment. Adjusted EBITDA margin of 30.7% outperformed the high end of guidance for a third consecutive quarter. This also translated to a new quarterly record of adjusted EBITDA dollars.

Finally, our strong free cash flow generation enabled targeted organic investments as well as capital return to shareholders. We are on pace to achieve our $90 million share buyback target for fiscal 2026. Looking back on the year, we made a steady arc of progress with improving fundamentals, tangible momentum, and an accelerating pace of innovation. Revenue and adjusted EBITDA have grown in tandem each quarter year to date. This largely resulted from deliberate reprioritization of Marketplace, our most scaled and differentiated asset. Unlocking Marketplace opportunities was the fastest way to inflect financial performance and help identify and drive the foundational changes needed to shift the long-term trajectory of the business.

These changes fall into the three categories we outlined on our February earnings call, each of which we've substantially advanced through the year. First, jumpstarting product innovation. We have meaningfully shortened development cycles, enabling us to quickly iterate on AI tools like Carson to stay ahead of changing consumer shopping habits. We also began the phased rollout of dealer-verified listings, which ties together the Marketplace and appraisal layers of our product platform for the first time. Launching new products can be long and iterative process, but our path is clear, and we are becoming a more interconnected and trusted Marketplace for consumers, dealers, and OEMs. Second, making sure we optimize our cost base and processes.

Shortly after I joined, we quickly made significant changes in April to reduce silos and management layers to speed growth and eliminate duplicated efforts. Other smaller organizational adjustments were also completed over the past few months to further align our resources to our roadmap. In aggregate, our ongoing cost containment efforts yielded $30 million-$35 million in discrete annualized operating cost savings. Third, and related, we are putting the right people in critical organizational roles. I am pleased to officially welcome Trent Ziegler, our new CFO, and Mausam Bhatt, our new Chief Product Officer. Both are seasoned professionals, adept at moving quickly to build leading digital businesses and marketplaces, trusted products, and interconnected product ecosystems.

We said before that the first step to powering the Marketplace flywheel is attracting and harnessing relevant inventory, such as affordable vehicles. Our surveys show that 50% of recent respondents are delaying a car purchase due to affordability. We identified a market gap we could meet, quickly invented, and built a new product that did not exist before, and we are seeing promising early results. Starter packages are an extremely timely addition to our portfolio as we attract local, smaller dealers whose lower-priced vehicles are exactly what consumers are seeking online.

Almost 400 dealers have already signed up for the starter package, and roughly 80% of vehicle inventory from starter dealers is under $20,000, squarely in the sweet spot for in-market shoppers. Practically speaking, this is also a highly efficient channel that requires zero sales or onboarding assistance before dealers begin listing with no fees. Although we are still making product changes and tweaks, more than 60% of eligible signups have been fully self-service. This is exactly in line with our emphasis on better, more scalable processes and a great example where we are doing more with less. Beyond offering more breadth of inventory, we have also improved how consumers find the right car using AI.

On platform, our Carson AI shopping assistant almost doubled its user base year-over-year to surpass 1 million monthly users during Q3. Our data clearly shows Carson's growing utility and trust among marketplace shoppers. Longer queries of six or more words have nearly tripled year-over-year. We also saw a 72% year-over-year increase in queries that only state vehicle needs without any OEM brand preference. This points to the significant opportunity for us to engage with consumers and provide them with tools and trust signals for their decision journey. Furthermore, around 91% of users rated Carson positively over the last six months. Carson is elevating the consumer experience on our platform.

Off-platform, third-party data shows that Carson continued to lead automotive marketplace peers in the number of citations by the largest LLMs in Q3. We are also in the process of integrating our MCP with Muse to surface our vehicle listings and dealers to more users. Overall, consumer scale and engagement on marketplace remains healthy and is trending up thanks to ongoing product improvements and optimization of marketing investments. Q3 traffic and visitors were down only mid-single digits year-over-year, a much lower decline versus Q1 and Q2. As a reminder, we intentionally shifted our focus to prioritize value delivery, target high-intent shoppers, and drive lead conversion.

We explained this during our last call, so we are pleased to report that lead performance was up nearly double digits year-over-year in Q3 and a direct result of more rigorous and targeted investments. Just as we saw last quarter, solid Q3 marketplace growth tells us that customers are responding well to our pivot. We took a disciplined approach to drive the metrics that truly matter for growth, and our strategy is working. Stepping back, we believe our marketplace has strengthened materially over the past nine months and is well-positioned for long-term growth. For consumers, listings today are more user-friendly, have more trust signals and AI integrations, and drive more engagement.

Proprietary data like dealer-verified listings and soon-to-come review badges, pricing breakdowns, and other features add to a richer Carson experience. These are long-term marketplace differentiators and key to sustaining our high brand recognition among car shoppers. Case in point, Q3 organic traffic volume grew year-over-year, and organic traffic as a percent of total traffic was at its highest level in nearly two years. For dealers and OEMs, we continue to advance product innovation such as VIN and lead-specific intelligence and AI solutions to drive more car sales. As I explained earlier, we strategically focused on marketplace first because it is our core.

Now, we are adapting the marketplace playbook and applying our product, process, and people tactics to transform our website business. Over the past six years, Dealer Inspire has grown from a disruptor into a scaled player, meaning future customer wins will hinge on product innovation rather than OEM endorsements. We have identified how to be a better partner to customers, and we are taking decisive action. In Q3, this work was behind the scenes, strengthening the foundation of our platform. Mobile site speeds have gotten more than 40% faster since spring, an important customer metric where we focused on moving the needle.

We launched inventory endpoints built for AI agents in May, and they have become one of the most visited parts of our platform as we help customers adapt to LLMs. We've also laid the groundwork to connect DI and cars.com to allow us to deliver a more personalized and unified consumer shopping experience. We pointed last quarter to adding current marketplace capabilities into DI, particularly related to AI. AI VIN videos, utilizing the technology that we showcased at NADA in February for marketplace and media customers, is coming to DI in Q4. Our native integration auto-generates vehicle summary videos for every vehicle on the lot to produce more engaging websites and signals with no additional overhead for dealers.

Leveraging the success of our Carson assistant on marketplace, similar AI shopper tools like search, recommendations, and VDP summaries will be embedded into DI websites in Q4. These are some of our ongoing improvements to make our websites best in class, and you'll see us continue to roll out enhancements steadily as part of our new platform roadmap. We are confident that we can stabilize website development and improve its growth outlook in 2027, as we have demonstrated for marketplace over the course of this year. In closing, I'd like to acknowledge both the important progress we've made since the start of the year and the work that is to come.

Recognizing the marketplace as our growth engine and reorienting the business to drive that flywheel meant a comprehensive overhaul of our strategy, investment, and organizational structure. Undertaking this hard work helped us return marketplace to year-over-year growth and its highest year-to-date revenue level in six years. Costs are down, while overall productivity and efficiency are up. We have filled key roles that will help push our growth and product agenda in 2027 and beyond. However, we are still in early innings, and several parts of our platform are not at their full potential. There will be near-term headwinds for point solutions like websites and trade and appraisal while we are working to reshape those roadmaps.

But we are energized by the work ahead and confident in the growth opportunities our strategy creates. Before we get into the financial results, and in light of our upcoming CFO transition, I want to take a moment to recognize Sonia and her many contributions to Cars.com over the past six years. She has been essential in driving the company forward, relentlessly finding avenues to improve performance and positioning us for success as we enter the next phase of our growth strategy. Not to mention, she has been an invaluable partner to me, as well as a leader and mentor across our organization.

We are glad that she'll be with us for a while longer to ensure a seamless handover to Trent. Thank you, Sonia. Now I'll turn it over to Sonia to discuss our financial results and outlook.

Sonia Jain: Thank you, Tobi. Being CFO of Cars has been a true honor. I am deeply appreciative of my talented colleagues and the finance team, and I am proud of what we have accomplished together. I also want to thank our investors and analysts for their support and partnership over the years. Cars is in good hands, and I look forward to seeing its continued transformation under Tobi and Trent. Now, turning to the financial discussion. In the third quarter, we executed on near-term growth opportunities while also delivering strong adjusted EBITDA and net income gains, with adjusted EBITDA outperforming our guidance range.

Our pace of product development continued to accelerate, with exciting launches like new starter packages adding momentum to our marketplace flywheel. Q3 revenue of $181.9 million was driven by similar dynamics as first-half performance. Subscription-based dealer revenue was up year-over-year for the fifth consecutive quarter. While OEM and national revenue recovered nicely from its Q2 trough, it was still down slightly year-over-year, weighing on total revenue growth. Further unpacking dealer revenue, our marketplace strategy continues to deliver from both a dealer footprint and listings growth perspective and value delivery that we are unlocking in the form of ARPD growth.

We extended our streak of growing marketplace customers in Q3 and exited the quarter with our second-highest subscription base in three years. With the launch of our new starter offering, we now also have the ability to offer marketplace capabilities to independent and smaller local dealers at no upfront cost. As Tobi mentioned earlier, there are numerous benefits to expanding beyond traditional subscription packages. The self-service aspect of the starter offering represents an efficient and scalable channel for acquiring listings inventory and also increases our presence with independent dealers. Between paid subscriptions and no-fee starter packs, we have added close to 600 independent dealers onto cars.com year-over-year.

ARPD grew another 3% year-over-year in Q3 to $2,532, just shy of a new record. The largest driver of growth was robust uptake of higher-tier marketplace subscriptions, such as Premium+. In May, we set out a goal to grow Premium+ adoption to 15% of mix by year-end, and I am pleased that we crossed the 12% mark in Q3. Marketplace progress, while very encouraging, was partially offset by challenges in dealer solutions and media products. Consolidated dealer count was down year-over-year in Q3 due to a decline in website subscriptions. We have been transparent about ongoing development work to augment our feature set and also better integrate platform capabilities into websites.

Upcoming AI-related enhancements for Dealer Inspire are just one example of our progress as we seek to return this part of our platform to healthier growth. We also made a deliberate decision to de-emphasize AccuTrade as a point solution in favor of more integration into Marketplace. Lastly, on revenue, OEM and national revenue was down 3% year-over-year and up 15% quarter-over-quarter in Q3. This performance was largely in line with our expectations, and we were encouraged to see improved spending by a majority of our OEM partners. Now, turning to our Q3 cost discussion. Third quarter operating expenses were $153 million, down 7% year-over-year. Roughly half of the year-over-year improvement stemmed from lower costs and improved efficiencies.

The remaining benefit resulted from lower depreciation and amortization expense following the full amortization of customer lists tied to our 2017 spin-off. Q3 adjusted operating expenses were $142.4 million, down 5% year-over-year from largely the same factors. For the following line item detail, all comparisons are on a year-over-year basis unless otherwise noted. Product and technology expenses were down low single-digit percentages on both a reported and adjusted basis. On balance, lower compensation expense was partially offset by slight increases in third-party software and hosting costs, netting out to a minimal year-over-year change.

Marketing and sales decreased roughly $2.9 million on a reported basis and $2.6 million on an adjusted basis, driven by more efficient marketing investments as we optimize our audience acquisition strategy to drive value delivery. General and administrative expense was down $3 million on a reported basis and up $1.6 million on an adjusted basis. The reported variance was primarily due to the expiration of the D2C earnout accrual. Recall that the D2C earnout accrual is excluded from adjusted operating expenses, which resulted in adjusted G&A expense increasing year-over-year from certain third-party costs.

As Tobi mentioned, our diligence on process and organizational optimization has yielded strong cost benefits in 2026 and also provides us with forward flexibility to reinvest resources to execute our new roadmap while preserving a portion of savings to benefit adjusted EBITDA. Third quarter net income was $16.3 million, or $0.30 per diluted share, compared to net income of $7.7 million, or $0.12 per diluted share a year ago. Net income was primarily driven by improved operating income. Adjusted net income for the third quarter was $32.3 million, or $0.58 per diluted share, compared to $30.4 million, or $0.48 per diluted share a year ago.

Adjusted EBITDA of $55.8 million in the third quarter was up 2% year-over-year, delivering robust operating leverage from steady gains in cost, process, and organizational efficiencies. Our resulting adjusted EBITDA margin of 30.7% overachieved the high end of our guidance range by 120 basis points. Moving on to cash flows and the balance sheet. Net cash provided by operating activities totaled $114.7 million for the nine-month period ending in Q3, compared to $114.5 million a year ago. Free cash flow was $97.3 million over that timeframe, up from $94.5 million a year ago. Share buybacks totaled 7.6 million shares for $74 million year-to-date through Q3, putting us well on pace to achieve our 2026 share repurchase target of $90 million.

Our 2026 buyback activity represents over 12% of the outstanding share count from the start of the year and reflects our commitment to return value to shareholders. In terms of debt, year-to-date total debt repayments of $10 million reduced total debt outstanding to $445 million as of September 30th, 2026. Total liquidity was $369.6 million as of September 30th, 2026, providing strong financial flexibility to support our growth priorities and other capital needs. Now, we'll conclude with outlook. We are reaffirming our full year 2026 guidance of flat to 2% revenue growth and adjusted EBITDA margin of 29%-30%. Bearing in mind our year-to-date performance and current trends, we expect revenue towards the lower end of our outlook range.

We anticipate tailwinds for Marketplace to persist, and we are pleased that our focused execution in 2026 has improved Marketplace's growth trajectory. We're acting with urgency to apply those product marketing and sales tactics to solutions and media products and move that portfolio from near-term declines back to stable to growing performance in 2027. The same is true on a smaller scale for OEM revenue, where we're assuming that near-term macro challenges will continue to temper media investments, but also see encouraging initial signals for 2027 spending commitments. For adjusted EBITDA, we are currently anticipating full-year performance to be at the higher end of our guidance range.

Proactive cost management and efficiency gains are yielding strong operating leverage that we expect to sustain through the remainder of the year. With that, I'd like to open the line for Q&A.

Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin the question and answer session. Should you have a question, please press the star followed by the one in your touchtone phone. Should you wish to cancel your request, please press the star followed by the two. If you are using a speakerphone, please lift the handset before pressing any keys. Your line is open.

Ethan Widell: Hi there. This is Ethan Widell on for Naved. Thanks for taking my questions. Could you maybe double-click on new traffic sources that you're exploring with agents and LLMs, and any early traction there? Thank you.

Tobi Hartmann: Hey, good morning. Yeah, thanks for your question. With regards to traffic to the website, I think we've outlined our strategy, which was that we would de-emphasize a little bit just driving traffic as opposed to driving leads. I think we're very happy that this strategy has worked. Traffic and UVs are recovering from first-half levels, and that we've seen we're de-emphasizing still the traffic, but we drove nearly double-digit increase on leads. You're basically seeing that the strategy on efficiency works. The other thing to mention is Carson. We had mentioned that we saw about 1 million users now, so it's really an embedded part now of our discovery search, and then leading to incremental engagement with users.

We are very pleased about that. The last point to close out is, we are also working on an integration with Muse that should follow in the next couple of weeks. We've had preliminary discussions and also some tests and trials, and that also looks promising. Thank you.

Ethan Widell: Thank you. That's helpful. Can you maybe tell us more about what you're seeing in OEM ad spend and maybe what your expectations are as we look towards 2027?

Sonia Jain: Yes, thank you for the question. We're pretty pleased to see the recovery in OEM spend from Q2 to Q3. We had mentioned that Q2 was going to be a trough, and we see good activity as we head into Q4 on the OEM side. We're not really giving formal 2027 guidance yet, but this is the time of year when we sit down with OEMs around upfront planning for their fiscal, and those conversations have been positive. I think one of the things we observed in Q3 is almost all of our OEM partners that we were working with were increasing spend levels.

So, it's nice to see them be a little bit more front-footed than we saw earlier in the year in how they are thinking about investing and investing in our platform.

Ethan Widell: Thank you. I appreciate all the color.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question is from Gary Prestopino from Barrington Research. Your line is open.

Gary Prestopino: Hi. Good morning, all. The self-service product for the independent dealer market, did I hear you right that there's no upfront charge for taking this on? If there isn't, what's the revenue stream?

Tobi Hartmann: Yeah, thank you for your question. You are correct. The self-service Marketplace Starter, as we call it, is focused on smaller, more local, and predominantly independent dealers. The idea is very simple. We follow the principle of listings traffic money, which means we need to have the relevant inventory on our marketplace. We saw that we had a gap, but there's a product need and there's a market need because due to the affordability issue in the U.S., there's more demand for, call it, more value offerings in terms of car segments. So, let's say up to $20,000, that's really a segment where we had not really a strong offering.

So, we're closing that product gap by bringing on those dealers literally as a self-service starter pack, so to say. Once they're on and once they experience the power of our marketplace, there's other solutions down the road that, for competitive reasons, I'd not like to talk about during this call, that we can then bundle and interconnect with going forward. But yes, you are correct. At first, it's a free, so to say, startup package to have them experience the power of our marketplace.

Gary Prestopino: Okay. Then, in terms of when you say it's self-service, I mean, how does it differ in the sense of what your normal Marketplace offering is to a franchise dealer? Exing out all the other add-ons that a franchise Marketplace dealer can get.

Tobi Hartmann: I'm glad you are asking that question. It's a great question. So, to be transparent, it's really new what we have built there, because self-service means that there is no handholding or hands on the keyboard that we need to enable and to get that partner or to get that local dealer started. In other words, we reach out to them, and they push a button, and everything pops in. Listings are populated. They see their inventory on Marketplace. They get a reporting, they get a cockpit, they get KPIs, and they are part of our ecosystem. That did not exist.

The way we operated before, and also for larger dealers, is there is a lot of handholding, there is a lot of manual processes in order to connect to the various systems, the dealer-related systems, the MarTech solutions, and so forth. It is a really, truly an innovative new product that the teams have put together, and the amount of time it took to put it together exceeded our own expectations. We are very pleasantly surprised, and we have about 60%-65% of all these new local smaller dealers using it as an auto service jumpstarted, as opposed to a manual process that we need to go through before. That really explains it. That's what we mean by self-service.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question is from Marvin Fong from BTIG. Your line is now open.

Marvin Fong: Great. Good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. I would like to also ask about the starter package. With other freemium products or free products that we see in the market, there are, like for instance, I believe, leads are anonymized and things of that nature. Are you doing a similar thing to incentivize these dealers to eventually upgrade to the subscription package? The second part of the question is, do you envision the next step for them your base package, or are you contemplating developing something in between, like the free package and the current standard package you offer to help them stay in the ecosystem and advance up the tier system?

Tobi Hartmann: Yeah. Thank you, Marvin. Highly relevant question. I should have mentioned that earlier, so I am glad you picked up on that. Yes, of course, just like with any other freemium products you see as a consumer that you are all absorbing in the market, there are certain caps and there are certain limitations as to how you can consume that free starter package. One of the dimensions, obviously, is our core currency in terms of leads and the number of leads we are providing, and that also ties to some product work we did, and we have accelerated in the past couple of months, which is the so-called DLE, the dealer lead engine.

We are getting more sophisticated in how we are distributing leads, how quickly we are distributing leads, and if you hop on as a new partner, obviously you would like to have a positive experience very early on. You wouldn't want to wait for three to four weeks for the first lead to come through. We are sophisticating our processes around that in terms of ramping up new customers, creating a positive experience, but then also telling them, "Hey, you are running into a cap, so now if you would like to stay on, you either have to upgrade or you got to talk to us." That is the journey that we are currently on.

The idea is that there is additional offerings wrapped around that in the spirit of interconnectivity, as I talked about in the past. The idea is that there are different levels in terms of caps. You could extend a cap or you could lower a cap. There is the idea of offering other services that are not directly tied to the pure marketplace, but that could be tied to the digital presence, i.e., the website, and/or also to a future program around verified. Thank you.

Marvin Fong: Got it. If I could do a follow-up, maybe for you, Sonia, just like on the financial impact or how should we think about the impact of the starter program on ARPD? I am assuming these dealers will be in the dealer count. They were in this quarter. Do you believe the ARPD might be affected or you can kind of overcome it?

Sonia Jain: I think in the very near term, and very specifically in terms of the Q3 numbers we have shared with you, the starter dealers are not included in our dealer count, and therefore are also not having an impact on ARPD. As you think about this longer term, I think the real thesis behind starter pack is, how do we get more listings onto our platform, particularly attractive, affordable listings? That is the primary goal. We do not view Starter Pack as a long-term driver of ARPD, because it will likely be dilutive to the ARPD calculation once we have the conversion feature built in.

This is largely oriented towards smaller independent dealers, but they are not included in the Q3 number. We do believe that this is a component of the overall marketplace flywheel, right? Listings bring eyeballs, which allow us to drive more value to both consumers and our customers.

Tobi Hartmann: Yeah. To build on what Sonia stated, we view this from two dimensions. We view this, one, in terms of there's a future impact through indirect monetization, which is what Sonia just alluded to. The more listings, the more inventory, the more market share we have down to townships, zip codes, DMAs, and so forth, dealership level value buckets, the more attractive the overall marketplace experience becomes, which leads to opportunities how you can monetize not directly, but indirectly through other parts of the ecosystem. The second one is the direct monetization layer that I touched on before, which is playing around with, throttles around lead caps, other caps, other services wrapped around and interconnectivity. Hope this clarifies it.

Marvin Fong: No, that was very helpful. Thank you. Sonia, best of luck on the future endeavors. Thanks.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question is from Josh Patel from JPMorgan. Your line is now open.

Josh Patel: Good morning, and thanks for taking my questions. Sonia, it has been a pleasure working with you, and best of luck. Congratulations on the continued product momentum. My first question is on transactional capabilities. With consumers increasingly embracing online vehicle purchases, as reflected in Carvana's growth and activity across other marketplaces, how are you thinking about Carson extending further into the transaction itself? Is there scope to accelerate investment in end-to-end purchasing capabilities? I think you mentioned an upcoming news integration, so maybe any additional flavor there would be very helpful. Thanks, and I have a quick follow-up.

Tobi Hartmann: Thanks. I will start off with that one. Another good question. The way we are thinking about our positioning and the future evolution is, we are really here not to compete with our customers. Anything that is more headed in the direction of buying or potentially getting really deep into the transaction itself, I would say right now is not core. Why not? Because our place to be is we want to be a trustworthy, a trusted, and authoritative partner to seekers, to buyers, to dealers, to OEMs, as a neutral platform partner that enables and empowers and facilitates our customers' transactions. That does not mean that we ourselves get into the transaction.

You should not expect us to see CapEx investments into picking up cars, selling cars, whatever, as opposed to really driving lead volume, driving highest quality of leads, driving innovation for local dealers, franchise, major dealerships, and helping them figure out how they can drive a better P&L. That is really our place to be.

Josh Patel: That is very helpful. Thank you. As a quick follow-up, the FTC pricing transparency enforcement has created a range of varied behaviors across the marketplace. I am wondering if you could just talk about how that has changed how dealers interact with Carson, how have they shifted their listing behavior, and what pricing trends are looking like. Thanks.

Tobi Hartmann: Yes. So, another really good question that lines up with what we just talked about, the positioning of our current platform and how we are thinking about it. We want to be consumer-led, to be clear, which means we are doing the right thing by the consumers. There will always be instances where customers, i.e. B2B customers, may have a different view because short-term, they will not share the same view, or they may say, "Look, there is hidden costs or expenses," and it is hard to transparently show all of that. But our mission and our job is to put everything on the platform to guide the consumers as part of a neutral marketplace, positive marketplace experience.

The changes that we implemented as part of the FTC requirements are largely welcome because it provides more transparency and it standardizes the way how B2B customers ought to interact with regards to price transparency. So, it is fully in line with our understanding of our role, our objectives, and we fully support this. Now, having said that, there will always be individual dealerships or individual customers who, for good or bad reasons, cannot make that happen overnight, and we also respect that because they are our customers. But we, as a platform operator, we want to do the right thing by the consumer.

Josh Patel: Understood. Great color. Thanks and good luck.

Operator: Your next question is from Joe Spak from UBS. Your line is now open.

Joe Spak: Thank you. Good morning, everyone. I was wondering if you could maybe help us think about how to size this opportunity, particularly as it relates to the Marketplace Starter packages. Because if I look at your dealer count, a little bit over 19,000, there's 40K U.S. franchise and independent dealers, but probably, what, 18K or so franchise. It's maybe almost half and half. I don't really have a good sense, I guess, for of your dealer exposure, maybe the share within each of those franchise versus independents. How much room do you think you have to go on the independent side from this initiative?

Tobi Hartmann: Yeah. Thank you. There's roughly, call it, probably north of 20,000 indies out there, and we are under-penetrated, clearly under-penetrated. What we'd like to bring across during this call, and as we will have further conversations with all of you in the next couple quarters, again, we don't want to call out, "Oh, this is a huge monetization potential right now," because it's part of an ecosystem approach. Again, there's a direct and there's an indirect monetization path. We believe this is strategically, operationally, and also for the long-term positioning of our marketplace absolutely crucial that we welcome these local dealerships, these independent dealerships.

We also think, as of today, that we have very specific assets in our portfolio that we can enrich the offering beyond a pure listings and marketplace experience that could be actually a pretty prominent USP. This is a part of our product roadmap for 2027. If you think about what's the opportunity, the opportunity is first inventory liquidity. We bring on additional inventory where we have data insights, what drives eyeballs, what drives the attractivity of a marketplace. The second piece is, we learn because we're getting additional signals in terms of supply and demand signals to connect the dots what it means to help consumers guide and take and make a better car decision.

The third piece is, as listings, pure listings, become more or less a commodity going forward, the question is, what's a listing going to be on our marketplace versus a listing on another marketplace? And there we have some cool things in store that we will develop over time, and we want to make sure that independent dealers and local dealers get access to that. We are developing it, if you will, from an enterprise-grade point of view, because we came from the large dealers, and they're the backbone, and they're really helping us think this through at the highest level of requirements and what's really needed to succeed in the market.

But then we're taking this down like an enterprise-grade level to the local dealerships, and that's why we think this is a powerful product path going forward.

Sonia Jain: And maybe, Joe, just to give you some numbers if you're trying to put some boundaries on this, we probably would say the mix is a little bit more heavily weighted to indies when you think about the overall TAM. So when you think about our dealer mix, we'll roughly call it two-thirds franchise, one-third independent, and that then translates into having, call it, like a 20%-25% penetration rate amongst independent dealers, which is why we're so excited about the opportunity with the starter package. It's a really efficient and scalable way for us to get after this segment.

Joe Spak: That's helpful. Maybe a quick follow-up on that and then sort of second question. Is there an opportunity for a somewhat similar package for larger dealers that are not currently using Cars.com? Then, the follow-on second question is just maybe, Sonia, specifically on the fourth quarter guidance, it's a pretty wide range since you didn't really sort of for EBITDA for the fourth quarter, since you didn't really touch the full year number. I think it's like plus or minus 10%. Just what would sort of You typically have pretty good visibility, but so I'm just curious sort of what would cause you to come in sort of higher end versus lower end. Thanks.

Sonia Jain: Yeah, maybe we'll take the guidance question first. So we did try to provide some indication. We've reaffirmed full year, but given where we are in terms of year-to-date performance, we expect to come in toward the lower end of that range on revenue and towards the higher end when it comes to adjusted EBITDA. I think there's a couple different puts and takes. Again, we've leveraged year-to-date performance in order to steer folks to the right portion of the guidance range. I would say Q4 is also an interesting time of year as people spend down their marketing budgets.

There's often opportunity for us to collect incremental dollars, particularly on the media side, which could move us maybe closer to the midpoint of the range. But what we're saying right now is given the information that we have today, we would expect to land towards the lower end of the revenue guide range.

Tobi Hartmann: Yeah, and your question regarding other customer segments and larger dealerships, it's really a different product. That's why we started from scratch. Our experience is, if you start to tweak your existing large enterprise kind of packages and say, "Okay, let's do the exact same thing, but now let's try to bring it down for smaller customers or local," that's one approach. From my experience, that's kind of hard to do. You got to start from scratch and almost start with a whiteboard and say, "Look, let's make this as convenient as possible, and let's think about what these customers really need." That's how we approached it.

There are more differences and nuances between our larger customers' packages and their subscription tiers versus the starter package. Now, having said that, we will learn from both ends. What we didn't talk about is, we've already collected great data signals from the engagement with those 400 dealerships that we just brought on recently, which will have an impact in terms of development cycle and innovation for the larger enterprise clients. It goes both ways, but they are different packages. They're different clients and customer segments, and they're different nuances in terms of obviously pricing and features.

#3260. Apple disables Siri AI waitlist in iOS 27, with one exception

When Siri AI launched in iOS 27 earlier this fall, Apple used a waitlist to gate access. But a newly updated support document says the waitlist is no longer being used, except in “high demand” times.

If you haven’t yet enabled Siri AI on your iPhone, Apple recently made it quicker and easier to gain access.

That’s because, per updates to this support document, the company is now only using a waitlist for Siri AI in “high demand” times.

After giving instructions on how to enable Siri AI by tapping “Try Siri AI (Beta)” inside Settings, here’s what the document used to say compared to what it says now.

This will add you to a waitlist, and wait times can vary. Siri AI will begin to download automatically when your wait is complete.

Siri AI will begin to download automatically. During time of high demand, you might be added to a waitlist first, and wait times can vary.

It’s understandable that a waitlist was used initially upon iOS 27’s release. Apple needed to slowly grant access while gauging server performance. But now that we’re nearly two months into the iOS 27 rollout, it’s great that Apple is only deploying the waitlist occasionally as needed.

Have you enabled Siri AI on your iPhone? If not, what’s holding you back? Let us know in the comments.

#3259. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.
