#3258. MacBook Pro OLED Review: The best display we've ever tested

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display impresses thanks to its astonishing touchscreen OLED display that’s the brightest we’ve ever seen on a laptop. On top of that, it has a thinner, lighter design, punchy speakers, and super-long battery life. Plus. Apple finally ditches the notch. While it’s very expensive, this marvelous laptop will floor you.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display ($2,899 to start) is the finest laptop I’ve had the pleasure of testing. There’s a lot of hype around Apple’s first touchscreen OLED MacBook, and I can tell you it far surpasses it. Though it commands a steep asking price, I’d argue that this laptop is worth every penny for the pros thanks to the excellent experience you get.

The tandem OLED panel is a stunner, delivering inky blacks and scorching bright whites. You instantly notice the 10 million-to-1 contrast ratio, which also makes colors pop. Then there’s the touch functionality, which is the most responsive I’ve used on any touchscreen laptop. Combine these features with the Dynamic Island (finally) replacing the notch, and you have the best display ever on a MacBook. This is especially true for models with the optional anti-glare nano-texture display.

Apple didn’t stop with the upgraded display, as this MacBook Pro also has a thinner, slimmer design than its siblings. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display weighs just a little more than a MacBook Air! You also get nearly 17 hours of battery life, blowing away the Windows competition. The cherry on top with the new design is the return of the iconic glowing Apple logo on the lid. In short, Apple somehow perfected its already stellar MacBook design.

While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is decidedly expensive with the same performance as the MacBook Pro laptops released in March 2026, it’s easily one of the best MacBooks and best laptops you can buy. If you can afford it, you won’t be disappointed. Find out more in my full review of the 14- and 16-inch OLED MacBook Pros.

14.2-inch PROLED XDR (3024 x 1986 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch

16.3-inch PROLED XDR (3472 x 2266 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch

M5 Pro (15-core CPU / 16-core GPU / 16-core Neural Engine)

M5 Pro (18 CPU cores, 20 GPU cores/ 16-core Neural Engine)

3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3

3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display offers a premium laptop experience, with a magnificent tandem OLED panel, elegant yet utilitarian design, and intuitive touchscreen controls. There’s a lot to love here.

MacBook Pros have used the same design since late 2021. Apple hasn’t radically redesigned the MacBook Pro OLED, retaining the sturdy, squared-off aluminum chassis with rounded edges. However, the new laptops are thinner and lighter than previous models—the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros weigh 0.5 and 0.7 pounds less, respectively, than their predecessors. If you use MacBook Pros as often as I do, you’ll feel the weight difference the instant you pick up either new laptop.

As before, you can open the lid with one hand. This is especially noteworthy because Apple redesigned the lids to better withstand constant tapping and swiping. The lid is also noticeably thinner yet remains very sturdy and doesn’t wobble. Apple has reduced the border size by 15%, resulting in thinner bezels. Lastly, the lid features the glowing Apple logo with a dedicated backlight, signaling to everyone that you’re using a PROLED MacBook Pro.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The keyboard looks and feels the same as on other MacBook Pros I’ve tested, which is great since they’re among the best laptop keyboards. Whether it’s the 14- or 16-inch model, the keyboard deck is spacious, and the keys are highly responsive, with excellent travel and just the right amount of resistance when pressed. The huge touchpad is also as great as ever, never failing to respond to my gestures. Speaking of touch, the Touch ID button is still here for easier logins. Unfortunately, Face ID is still not supported.

You get the same array of ports here, including three Thunderbolt 5/USB-C ports, an HDMI port, a 3.5mm headphone jack, an SD card slot, and a MagSafe charging port.

Pardon the cliché, but the panel on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a feast for the eyes. Even our lab tester, who tests the best TVs for a living, said he has never seen a lovelier display! I wholeheartedly agree.

The latest trailer for Dune: Messiah showcases what makes the PROLED’s panel such a marvel. The superb contrast renders nighttime scenes appropriately dark, while Arakis’ scorching sun makes you squint during daytime sequences. I’m also impressed by the level of detail on the characters’ dusty faces, thanks to the sharp resolution of both models.

549.8% (SDR) | 1949 (HDR, 10% of display)

Our lab tests confirmed what my eyes saw. Apple claims the PROLED MacBook Pros can reach 2000 nits of brightness, and our display benchmarks were just a hair under that mark. The brightest laptop displays we’ve tested topped out at 1600 nits, but Apple’s notebooks go well beyond that. It’s even more impressive when you consider that images remain clearly defined even when portions of the display are set to maximum brightness.

Color reproduction (sRGB and DCI-P3) is identical on the two PROLED laptops. Color accuracy (Delta-E) is slightly better than on most of the laptops I’ve tested. Combined with the 10 million-to-1 contrast ratio, you get truly exceptional display quality.

Moving away from benchmarks, let’s discuss the other major display upgrade—the removal of the notch at the top center. While I’ve never been too bothered by the notch, I’m not sad to see it replaced with the Dynamic Island, which makes it easy to access Live Activities. I like how the Dynamic Island expands when you’re playing videos and music, and how you can use the touchscreen to stop playback, fast-forward, and rewind.

The PROLED MacBook Pro with M5 Pro supports up to three external displays (up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), or one display up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz paired with a second up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz. The M5 Max model steps this up to four external displays (up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), or two displays up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz.

Both chips can power the laptop's built-in PROLED XDR screen at full resolution at the same time. Thanks to Thunderbolt 5’s native DisplayPort 2.1 bandwidth, you can connect three or four external monitors through a single port using compatible docks or daisy-chaining.

As we detailed in our 10 things you need to know about the MacBook Pro OLED, most laptops use a separate, distinct digitizer to support touch input. Apple found a way to integrate the touch silicon directly into these laptops’ tandem OLED displays. The result? A super precise touchscreen experience.

I’ve tested dozens of Windows touchscreen laptops, but none have felt as responsive or intuitive as on the MacBook Pro OLED. Because of that, tapping, swiping, and even pinch-to-zoom are as smooth and snappy as on an iPad Pro.

I’ve tested dozens of Windows touchscreen laptops, but none have felt as responsive or intuitive as on the MacBook Pro OLED. Because of that, tapping, swiping, and even pinch-to-zoom are as smooth and snappy as on an iPad Pro. I didn't notice any input lag. Menu bar items expand under your fingertip, and window controls get bigger, making things easier to see and interact with.

So far, I haven’t encountered any compatibility issues with third-party apps. Google apps, such as Docs and Drive, work well with touch based on my testing. And naturally, Apple’s own apps work seamlessly. I’ll keep testing to see if I run into any issues, but so far macOS seems like a natural fit for touch.

I don’t often use touch controls on laptops with touchscreens because they can feel clunky, but I found myself using the MacBook Pro’s touch controls more than I expected. That’s a testament to how well touch is implemented on these laptops.

MacBook Pros have always featured excellent speakers that deliver incredible sound, but even that experience didn’t prepare me for how amazing the speakers are on the new MacBook Pro OLED laptops.

Apple says the enhanced six-speaker sound system now delivers 50 percent deeper bass. And that’s not just marketing bluster. It was the first thing I heard, or rather, felt, when I fired up Tommy Johansson’s cover of Black Sabbath’s “Headless Cross.” The rumbling bass notes beneath the ripping solos and soaring vocals made it feel like a live performance—and no doubt annoyed my neighbors when I had the volume cranked up.

The movie trailer for the latest Godzilla Minus Zero also sounds spectacular on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Explosions, screams, and Godzilla’s iconic roar all came through loud and punchy. And naturally, voices in dialogue-heavy content like the Triple K.O. podcast also sound impressive.

Speakers can almost feel like an afterthought on some laptops, but that’s certainly not the case here. Whether it’s the 14- or 16-inch MacBook Pro, your ears won’t be disappointed. The sound system on these laptops is every bit as impressive as the display.

Even if the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in the new OLED MacBook Pros aren’t technically new like the Apple M6 chip, they’re still the most powerful M-series chips available for MacBooks. Since these are the same chips we’ve already tested on the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros from March, these laptops deliver comparable performance.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display Apple sent us (valued at $3,699 as configured) has an M5 Pro chip with an 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU, 48GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and a glossy display.

Meanwhile, the 16-inch model I reviewed (valued at $8,549) packs an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU / 40-core GPU, 128GB of RAM, a 4TB SSD, and a nano-texture display. Thanks to those specs, both laptops pack a serious performance punch.

Geekbench AI (Quantized Core ML/Neural Engine)

On the Geekbench CPU benchmark, both the 14- and 16-inch PROLEDs delivered strong single- and multi-core scores. They also scored well in Geekbench’s AI benchmarks.

As you can see above, OLED touchscreen competitors like the Dell XPS 16 (currently $2,469) and Lenovo Yoga 9n (currently $2,999) don’t come close in performance. For your reference, the XPS 16 packs an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, while the Yoga 9n has an Nvidia RTX Spark N1X chip, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD.

Surprise, surprise, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also crushed it in our other benchmarks. Disk speeds are extremely zippy, and the same is true for video transcoding. In fact, the new MacBook was more than 2x as fast as the Dell XPS 16.

Apple’s MacBook PROLED laptops are also more than capable of handling tasks in Adobe creative apps like Photoshop and Premiere Pro. Again, the competition can’t keep pace with Apple’s notebooks.

3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited (score / fps)

The PROLEDs aren’t slouches at gaming. On the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited GPU benchmark, the laptops scored well, with the M5 Max model performing significantly better thanks to its beefy 40-core GPU. The RTX Spark-powered Yoga 9n didn’t do badly, but Apple’s Pro laptops still outclassed it in this benchmark.

For real-world gaming, I tested Cyberpunk 2077 on both PROLED models. With the “For This Mac” graphics setting, the game ran at 85 fps and 95 fps, respectively. Cyberpunk 2077 is a graphically demanding game that pushes even powerful PCs to their limits, so these results are very impressive.

MacBooks with M-series chips are among the longest-lasting laptops we’ve ever tested. But I wasn’t expecting this kind of endurance, since there appears to be no “power penalty” for Apple adding an OLED touchscreen.

In Tom’s Guide’s battery life test, which involves continuous web surfing over Wi-Fi with the display set to 150 nits of brightness, the 14-inch MacBook Pro PROLED lasted 16 hours and 56 minutes, while its 16-inch counterpart endured 21 hours and 24 minutes. The previous non-touch 16-inch MacBook Pro M5 Pro lasted 21:10. This is yet another test in which Windows laptops are handily outclassed.

We always run three battery tests to calculate an average time, but we could only run one test in time for this review. I’ll update once we’ve completed the full testing, but based on my experience, the final results will be just as epic.

The webcam on the new PROLED MacBooks is mostly the same as before, only with a new stabilization feature to prevent screen wobble if you’re actively using the touchscreen display. As before, the camera can record 1080p video and also has Desk View.

The 12-megapixel Center Stage camera is as great as ever. This photo I took in my apartment late at night captures all the details on my face, clothing, and even in my background. During a Google Meet session, colleagues on the call also said my video looked sharp.

The new MacBook Pros come with macOS Golden Gate installed. Like I said in my macOS Golden Gate review, this update isn’t a complete overhaul like macOS Sequoia, but it brings a slew of new and enhanced AI features and smoother overall performance that make using MacBooks feel more personal and streamlined.

macOS Golden Gate now includes a dedicated Siri AI app that works like a typical chatbot. In a dedicated chat window, you can ask Siri AI questions or talk to it about whatever’s on your mind. Siri is baked into the OS, so it can recognize what’s on your screen and do things like add items to your calendar or create shortcuts by speaking what you want instead of building them manually.

A new Liquid Glass UI slider lets you adjust the effect’s opacity more precisely. You’ll also notice that complex background visuals appear more diffused, improving text readability. Icon edges are more pronounced so they stand out more. This feature should have been in Sequoia, but at least it’s here now in Golden Gate.

Another highlight of macOS Golden Gate is Spatial Reframing, which is also available on iOS and iPadOS. Reframe lets you reframe existing photos and adjust the perspective to your liking. If you’ve taken a lot of photos with your iPhone or iPad, this feature is a great way to make them look exactly how you want.

macOS Golden Gate goes big on AI, especially with the new and improved Siri. If that doesn’t matter to you, you’ll still enjoy a smooth, stable macOS experience overall.

The new OLED MacBook Pros are easily the most impressive laptops I’ve ever tested, but all those amazing features come at a steep cost.

I wasn’t expecting the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display to be cheap, given all the high-end components it uses. That said, I can’t help but wonder how much these laptops would have cost without RAMageddon inflating electronics prices. I suppose that doesn’t matter, because in this reality, you’ll have to pay a premium for Apple’s high-end touchscreen laptop.

Tech enthusiasts or anyone who can be more productive with a touchscreen laptop will get their money’s worth with the PROLED MacBook Pros. If you want to save money on a MacBook Pro and don’t need the performance of the M5 Pro/M5 Max chips, or if an OLED touchscreen isn’t important to you, the new M6-powered 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. That’s also expensive, but still $900 less than the entry-level MacBook Pro PROLED.

Since the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the regular MacBook Pros we’ve tested, performance gains are negligible at best. This matters if you're considering upgrading from those MacBook Pros to the new touchscreen laptops.

Geekbench AI (Quantized Core ML/Neural Engine)

3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited (score / fps)

I selected some benchmarks I discussed earlier to show you how these MacBook Pros compare in performance. As you can see, the gains are minor at best. So unless you are set on owning a touchscreen OLED MacBook, it might be wiser to save your money for future iterations that deliver a substantial performance boost over what you currently own.

I thought the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display could be amazing, but it shattered and exceeded my expectations. The new tandem OLED display raises the bar for laptops in brightness and color reproduction. Smooth touchscreen controls, a lighter design, and booming audio take Apple’s new machine to the next level. Yes, it’s very expensive, but it’s a brilliant laptop that makes competitors pale in comparison.

Apple’s first attempt at a touchscreen MacBook is mostly a success, but I’m already curious to see what future iterations bring to the table. If this initial laptop is anything to go by, we’re in for some truly fantastic devices. For now, Apple has made good with these laptops. They truly are the best of the best.

#3257. Apple Photos keeps getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

iOS 27’s biggest highlight is Siri AI, but the update also packs new features for apps like Messages, Notes, Wallet, and more. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Photos app in iOS 27.

Apple Intelligence powers a trio of editing tools in iOS 27’s Photos app: Extend, Reframe, and a much-improved Clean Up feature.

Extend lets users “give their subjects more breathing room,” per Apple. For example, “they can straighten a crooked horizon without cropping out anything important, or adjust the aspect ratio, and Extend will fill in the missing pieces.”

Reframe lets you adjust the framing of your image spatially. Here’s how Apple describes it:

With Spatial Reframing, users can improve the composition of a photo after it’s been taken. Spatial Reframing builds on Apple’s deep understanding of spatial models thanks to Apple Vision Pro, so users can touch and drag a photo and preview in real time how the perspective shifts — as if they’d repositioned the camera in the original scene. Using powerful image models, Spatial Reframing will only generate new content where the perspective has been shifted, ensuring the reframed photo stays consistent with the original scene.

And the Clean Up feature that debuted in iOS 18 “gets a major upgrade,” Apple says, “so users can remove distractions with better quality and more realistic infill, even when the scene is complex.”

iCloud Shared Albums get their first major upgrades in years with iOS 27. The timing is likely no coincidence, with the feature perfect for Apple’s new HomeView product.

Here’s an overview of what’s new, per Apple:

iOS 27 adds two new collections to the Photos app, available under Utilities.

Captured by Me exclusively contains photos taken by you. So it will filter out screenshots, photos you’ve saved from others, and so on.

Identity Documents scans through your Photos library and surfaces images that contain important reference documents, like your driver’s license or passport.

Apple says iOS 27 also adds “Album organization improvements,” but it doesn’t mention specifics.

Another new organization tool in iOS 27 is that you can add keywords to photos. Captions are still available too, but if you scroll up on a photo, near the bottom you’ll find a new ‘Add Keywords’ option.

Another upgrade perfect for HomeView involves slideshow improvements.

Apple Photos has supported quick, easy slideshow creation for years. But if you wanted to customize the automatically generated slideshows, you were out of luck.

Now in iOS 27, slideshows offer new tools for customization. You can change the transition type, set a custom length for the full slideshow and for each photo, and more.

Another welcome addition is that Apple now lets you save any slideshow as a video with one tap.

iOS 27 doesn’t contain any big changes to the design of the Photos app, so if you were hoping to go back to the pre-iOS 18 era, you’ll be disappointed. But the update does offer a variety of exciting new features that make iOS 27 a big release for Apple Photos.

Which of iOS 27’s new Apple Photos features are your favorites? Let us know in the comments.

#3256. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

With one official announcement and one report, two new Apple TV projects have been revealed this week. Here are the details.

This will mark Timberlake’s second project at Apple TV, after “Palmer,” a 2021 drama about an ex-convict who befriends a boy from a troubled home.

One source says the series will feature Janet Jackson discussing the infamous “wardrobe malfunction” that took place during the pair’s performance at the 2004 Super Bowl. Another source says that Timberlake discusses some of former girlfriend Britney Spears’ recent comments as well.

Here’s Apple TV’s synopsis of the new show:

“Lenni” is a darkly comedic mystery about family — what it means to have one, to lose one, to pull one apart. Lenni, a child welfare worker and divorced mother of two, spends her days fighting for other people’s families while her own is in a constant state of hilarious chaos. Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

#3254. Insurer Guardian hands 1 million dental calls a year to Sierra’s AI agents

The US insurer will also use Bret Taylor's startup for payments and claim status questions.

Guardian Life signed a multi-year deal with Sierra to use its AI agents for about 1 million dental benefit verification calls a year, plus payments and claim status checks. It is Guardian’s third AI partnership in a year, after HCLTech and Avantos.

US insurer Guardian Life is handing some of its busiest customer service work to AI agents from Sierra, the startup run by former Salesforce co-chief executive Bret Taylor. The two signed a multi-year partnership, Guardian said on Thursday.

Guardian will use Sierra for about 1 million calls a year to check dental benefits, plus payments and questions about claim status. It says the aim is faster answers, but it has not shared any targets or financial terms. Sierra has argued that AI agents should be paid per result, not per seat.

“No one should have to sit on hold to check on a claim or confirm dental benefits,” said Taylor, Sierra’s chief executive and co-founder.

Michael Prestileo, Guardian’s chief strategy officer, said the deal would let staff focus on the cases where “human judgment and connection matter most.”

It is Guardian’s third AI deal in a year. In July, it signed a seven-year deal with HCLTech, which is taking over Guardian’s India centre and nearly 2,000 of its staff. In February, it invested in Avantos, an AI platform for financial advisers.

Sierra, launched in February 2024, says it works with 46% of the Fortune 50. It raised $950M at a $15B valuation in May. Rivals are consolidating: Salesforce, which Taylor once co-ran, is buying Fin for $3.6B.

It has been adding features fast. Last month, it teamed up with Stripe so its agents can take card payments during calls, and with Meta on an open standard for personal AI agents.

Enrollment restarts as cash burn rises and partnership talks advance.

Intensity Therapeutics, Inc. (INTS -11.43%) reported the resumption of clinical enrollment in its late-stage sarcoma and breast cancer programs following previous delays related to funding and protocol revisions. Management reported that the company's phase III INVINCIBLE-3 study is currently enrolling patients at U.S. sites with plans to expand to Europe and Canada in early 2027. Furthermore, the content of this conference call contains time-sensitive information that is accurate only as of the date of this live broadcast, November 5th, 2026. Except as required by law, the company disclaims any intention or obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements. I'll now turn the call over to Mr. Bender, Intensity's President and CEO.

Lewis Bender: Thank you, Wyatt, and thank you, everyone, for joining us this morning. It is my pleasure to provide the latest update of our company's progress in the INVINCIBLE-3 and INVINCIBLE-4 studies, our publications and presentation strategy, our business development activities, and our plans for the rest of 2026 into 2027. First, I will turn the call over to Joe Talamo, our CFO, to discuss our third quarter financial results. Joe?

Joseph Talamo: Thanks, Lou, and good morning. I'm pleased to join you today and to present a summary of our third quarter 2026 financial results. Our research and development expenses were $2.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with $1.6 million for the same prior year period, reflecting an increase of $876,000, or 56%. Clinical trial expenses for our phase III INVINCIBLE-3 study were $1.5 million during the third quarter of 2026, compared with $1 million for the same prior year period. In the current year quarter, we resumed new patient enrollment activities in the INVINCIBLE-3 study in a limited number of U.S. sites after pausing new site activations and patient enrollment in March 2025 due to funding constraints.

During this pause, we continued to treat and monitor patients previously enrolled in the study in cooperation with our CROs. We have prioritized commencing full patient enrollment and site activations once sufficient incremental funding is obtained. Our clinical trial expenses also included $104,000 for our phase II INVINCIBLE-4 study, which also resumed patient enrollment and treatment in the third quarter of 2026. We expect the INVINCIBLE-4 study costs to increase in the coming quarters as we target completing enrollment in this study by the end of 2027. Lou will provide an operational update on both studies shortly. During the third quarter of 2026, we also initiated a new manufacturing batch of INT230-6, incurring $162,000 in higher manufacturing costs.

We expect this batch will be completed in the first quarter of 2027 and will likely be sufficient to fully supply both ongoing clinical studies. Lastly, research and development employee compensation-related expenses were $184,000 higher during the current quarter due to an estimated bonus accrual in the current year period, compared to no bonus accrual in the prior year period. Turning now to G&A. General and administrative expenses were $1.3 million for the third quarter of 2026 and were unchanged compared with the same prior year period. Within G&A, minor increases in employee compensation-related expenses and consulting expenses were offset by minor decreases in insurance costs during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same prior year period.

Overall, net loss was $3.5 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with a $2.7 million loss for the third quarter of 2025, representing an increase in net loss of $873,000, or 33%. Our cash burn from operating activities for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $6.7 million, reflecting an average monthly operating activities cash burn of $741,000 over the first nine months of 2026. We estimate that our operating cash burn will average approximately $1 million per month in the final quarter of 2026 as we continue to advance our clinical studies and manufacture the new INT230-6 batch. Turning now to our balance sheet.

As of September 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $8.5 million. During the third quarter of 2026, we raised $1.5 million in net proceeds from the issuance of common stock under our at-the-market facility. For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we raised $3.2 million in net proceeds under the at-the-market facility. We expect to continue to use this facility opportunistically to raise capital, and we will continue to explore other sources of dilutive and non-dilutive capital as we seek to scale up our clinical activities moving forward. With that, I will now turn the call back to Lou for a discussion on our clinical programs and business development activities. Lou?

Lewis Bender: Thank you, Joe. Well, we are pleased to hold today's earnings call following the positive feedback we received from our stockholders and stakeholders after last quarter's call. Today, as I said, I will discuss the continued progress that the company has made this quarter in more detail and provide an update on ongoing activities. As you just heard from Joe, we ended the third quarter with about $8.5 million. In the fourth quarter, we continue to evaluate the opportunities to raise capital via the ATM and other types of offerings or financings as opportunities present themselves to us.

Well, now I'm going to update on the phase III INVINCIBLE trial, which is our open-label, randomized controlled clinical study that is testing our drug INT230-6 as monotherapy, meaning just our drug alone, compared to the best standard of care drugs in second and third line treatment for three types of soft tissue sarcomas. On last quarter's call, we reported that we had initiated new patient enrollment in terms of starting the process for that in the INVINCIBLE-3 study in a limited number of U.S. sites.

To make this restart happen, this quarter, we added new CROs to help manage this clinical study, including vendors for statistical analysis and a large organization that specializes in receiving computed tomography, known as CT, images from sites around the world electronically during clinical trials. The purpose of this change is to establish consistency of the reads by radiologists across all sites, whether a patient's cancer is progressing or not, or regressing, compared to a patient's prior scan. Our key sarcoma thought leaders made a few important observations and recommendations. One was a central read, and the other was a recommendation to use a different set of criteria to determine whether a patient's disease was progressing.

In the prior version of the amended protocol, we based disease progression on tumor size, which is standard practice for systemic treatments. However, we have learned for our drug, the tumor becomes larger from the injection, from immune cell infiltration, and from the buildup of fluid as the cancer cells die. While changes in tumor size using criteria such as RECIST or WHO may be standard practice for determining progression for systemic treatments because it's based on the size of the tumor, we believe those criteria are unsuitable for our unique intratumoral drug.

Working with the expert radiology group, we finalized a set of criteria to assess whether a patient's cancer is progressing by measuring the tumor's density compared to its baseline. These criteria are referred to as Choi, and they are often used for certain types of sarcoma. While size goes up, density declines using our drug, and using Choi, we think we will have a better assessment of progressive disease. The endpoint remains overall survival. Sites will send their scans for assessment to the central review group, who will return a report on the Choi scores and provide detailed information on density changes for treated and untreated tumors.

Recruitment began in the U.S. in Q3 enrollment, and several sites are activated and seeking patients. We've also filed the needed documentation to restart the phase III in Europe and Canada in Q3. We expect to have approval to begin under the amended protocol in Europe in Q1. As we've mentioned, as incremental capital is raised, we will assess the timing of when additional sites can be activated in the U.S., the E.U., and Canada. Moving to ESMO now. Last month, Kim Guedes, our Vice President of Clinical Operations, and I traveled to Madrid to attend the Annual European Society for Medical Oncology Conference, known as ESMO.

We met with several of the INVINCIBLE-3 investigators who remain excited to resume their participation in the study. The last drug approved for second or third line soft tissue sarcoma of the types in our study was in 2016. It's been a long, dry desert for these patients. The three-year survival for sarcoma patients at this stage with progression, when we will begin to treat, is low. It's in the single digits. The physician investigators told us that there is an opportunity, given the lack of trial options for these patients, for new therapies. We are motivated to activate sites, enroll, and determine whether INT230-6 can help sarcoma patients live longer with improved safety and better quality of life.

Capital is the restriction on speed. Now provide an update on our phase II INVINCIBLE-4 presurgical breast cancer study, which is our randomized, controlled, open-label, multicenter study of INT given before the administration of standard of care neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy regimen in patients with early-stage operable triple-negative breast cancer. The efficacy endpoint is pathological complete response, referred to as pCR, which is the absence of any live cancer at the time of surgery in the tumor, breast, or lymph nodes. Tumor sizes in our trial are more challenging to treat, as our inclusion criteria uses a larger minimal tumor size than what was used for approval of the current regimen. Larger tumors are more challenging to treat.

On October 23rd, we announced new data at ESMO on patients who received our drug, showing an early indication of the potential to improve the percentage of women achieving a pathological complete response, or pCR. Clinical studies have shown that if triple-negative breast cancer patients have no live cancer at the time of surgery, the pCR, the risk of the disease returning in five years after surgery is significantly reduced, from about 50% without having a pCR to about 16% with a pCR. This difference is clinically meaningful, and many regulatory agencies, including the U.S. FDA and the EMA, accept pCR as an endpoint for certain types of accelerated or conditional approvals. There are two cohorts in the study.

The first is one dose of our drug administered prior to the standard of care. This is cohort A. The second cohort B, is the standard of care alone. Patients are randomized one-to-one to each cohort. As reported previously, 71% of patients who received INT230-6 achieved a pCR compared to 42% the standard of care. Very small numbers, it's early data. But these were patients with a median tumor size of 2.6, which is quite large. We also reported that no invasive cancer cells were detected in the axillary lymph nodes in six of the seven patients in cohort A after INT230-6 treatment, despite five of these seven patients, 71%, being initially biopsy-proven node positive. We don't know the nodes.

Results also showed tumor necrosis in all seven cohort A patients. In the pre-surgery MRI, at the completion of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy, four patients in our group had radiological complete response, and three patients, 43%, had partial response. All seven patients met criteria for breast-conserving surgery. These surgical results are consistent with the results from the study in Ottawa, our completed INVINCIBLE-2 study, that the timing of the surgery is unaffected by the use of our drug, which is a very important factor for patients.

We resumed to dose new patients in the third quarter in INVINCIBLE-4 after the study enrollment was paused late last year to revise the dosing regimen for patients receiving our drug because some patients experienced localized skin issues. Our collaborators in the INVINCIBLE study, the Swiss Cancer Institute, have established an IDMB of qualified experts to review safety data and images from these newly treated patients and assess whether the skin issues have been resolved.

The institute team felt, and we agreed, that an independent group of experts reporting that the current dosing regimen had resolved the skin issue would be the best way to assure all the investigators of the safety of this drug with regards to the skin issue. As a side note, we used a higher dose for tumor size in our completed INVINCIBLE-2 study in Ottawa compared to the revised dosing regimen in the ongoing INVINCIBLE-4 study. In the first study, 60 women received our treatment, and no skin issues were reported when injections were made with ultrasound to guide the needle. The INVINCIBLE-4 study uses higher quality ultrasound than was used in the INVINCIBLE-2.

After ESMO, I met and went to Switzerland and met with several of the sites. The meetings included the investigators, the nursing teams, coordinators, pharmacists, and other staff. I presented background data on INT230-6, the data from the Ottawa study, the latest safety and efficacy data from the ongoing phase II INVINCIBLE-4 study, and new results presented at ESMO. I was encouraged by our discussions and the investigators' enthusiasm to enroll their TNBC patients at each site. At ESMO, we also met with our partners at the group managing the French sites, UNICANCER. Along with a couple of French investigators, we discussed the science and study data. Several sites in France have had their site initiation visit and are activated.

We also plan to visit the sites in France, and the remaining sites in Switzerland after the independent safety report is available. We hope to give investigators confidence that a single injection of our drug has the potential to improve efficacy, be safer, and provide patients with the same skin appearance with our drug or without it. These efforts allow us to continue to target completion of enrollment by the end of 2027. It's also important to remember that using today's best immunochemotherapy regimens, only about 50%-63% of TNBC patients achieve a pCR. This depends highly on the size of the tumor. Half a percent of women die from the current approved regimen.

Preliminary findings on safety and efficacy from this randomized control study are encouraging to us and our European investigators. I would now like to discuss our clinical publication efforts. Last quarter, I discussed the 2025 eBioMedicine paper, which focused on translational science of using our drug alone. We continue to pursue additional peer-reviewed manuscript publications from our completed studies to further communicate the important clinical data and results to the oncology community. We have submitted a manuscript to a quality journal from our INVINCIBLE-2 breast cancers trial, and another manuscript from our IT-01 study in metastatic cancer of our drug with immunotherapy to another journal.

The journal's editors accepted each manuscript for peer review, and we have received reviewer comments, which we are addressing. Assuming our responses satisfy the reviewers and editors, we hope to see the papers published next year before Q2. Lastly, we continue to pursue potential partnerships in order to advance our programs more quickly and effectively. While the process is still early, we are pleased with the interest in our science and clinical trials, and discussions continue with several companies. We have also engaged a senior business development consultant to provide supplemental outreach and additional support.

To summarize, our cash position is good, we have options to increase capital, our clinical studies are advancing, and we have reinitiated patient enrollment in both late-stage programs. New peer-reviewed clinical publications are in process, and partnering business development discussions continue. This time, I would like to open the call up to questions.

Operator: We will now begin the question and answer session. To ask a question, you may press star, then one on your touchtone phone. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. To withdraw your question, please press star, then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. The first question will come from Kumar Raja with Brookline Capital. Please go ahead.

Kumar Raja: Thanks for taking my questions, and congratulations on all the progress. First, with regard to the INVINCIBLE-4 study, what specific safety endpoints or the metrics will the IDMB looking at in Q1, and what would give confidence that the localized skin irritation has been resolved?

Lewis Bender: Yeah. Thank you, Kumar, for the question. They are looking at the surface of the skin, whether or not there is any irritation over a period of several months. The patients have been enrolled, we are following them for a number of months. We are going to stop after a certain number of patient months. It is coming up very soon. They are just simply going to look and see if the issues that we saw before, and did not see in INVINCIBLE-2, with this new dosing regimen, exist or not. It is that simple.

It is looking at the images of the skin and probably some other metrics that they have, but nothing other than a simple visual, I think, is the key criteria for them.

Kumar Raja: Okay. You also hinted a little bit about business development. Can you provide any color on the nature of this discussion? Anything you can share with regard to that?

Lewis Bender: Well, we have been discussing with regional players, we have been discussing with multinational players. We are still in the evaluation part of this. We have a data room, there are CDAs in place, we are in discussion about the programs. What is of interest to these companies is both programs in some cases, one or the other program in other cases. There are multiple discussions, multiple topics.

We are really in the get to know each other stage right now, but I can tell you that the interest in a phase III program and phase II program in breast cancer, where it is a single dose and a phase III program in a rare disease like sarcoma, which has literally nothing really for 10 years of any consequence, is of interest to these companies.

Kumar Raja: Okay, great. Finally, with regard to the INVINCIBLE-3, what are your expectation in terms of getting additional sites activated? Thank you.

Lewis Bender: Well, as I said, we have opened a number of sites. We are looking for patients. As Joe has said, it will be in a gated way so that we can manage enrollment as we bring in capital. We do not want to get our skis ahead of ourselves and enroll too quickly, which we could possibly do, before we have the adequate cash. Capital will be the gating factor on how quickly we enroll. The enthusiasm is there. We have maintained almost all of the sites over the last, I would say, year and a half since we paused the study. Contracts are in place, budgets are in place.

We had almost 32 sites with contracts agreed and another 30 sites with contracts in negotiation when we paused. We could enroll quickly, or quicker than what we are planning, as we get more capital. It is really going to be definitive on the capital raising that we do.

Operator: Your next question will come from Charles Wallace with H.C. Wainwright. Please go ahead.

Charles Wallace: Hi, this is Charles on for RK. Thanks for taking my question. I guess first from me, for the INVINCIBLE-3 study, you mentioned several sites were active and patients identified. I was just curious if any of the patients have been randomized at this point, and how many sites do you expect to have open by year end?

Lewis Bender: Patients have not yet been randomized. They're going through an evaluation and screening process to make sure they meet all the suitable enrollment criteria that we have. There are a number that have been identified, but that's a process that takes a little bit of time. Ultimately, we will have about 10, we think, initially enrolling, but ultimately, the number of patients we can accept is really going to be dependent on the capital.

Charles Wallace: Okay. Yeah, that makes sense. I guess another question on INVINCIBLE-3. You mentioned the switch to the density-based CT image. Will that just be for the active arm or also the standard of care comparator? Or will the standard of care still use the size-based image?

Lewis Bender: So, it's for both arms. Obviously, it has to be for both. In Choi, there is an element of RECIST, right? So, what you have is, if you're measuring the size increase and the density change. If there's no density change and the size increases, then it's a PD, right? So, it's the same for both groups because they have to use one criteria for both groups. Seeing in our drug a Choi score for the tumors that we've selected for the Choi measurements, a density decrease but a size increase, and the density decrease is above 15%, even if the size increase is really high, it's a PR by Choi.

Because density is really what we're looking at trying to control, because that means that there's no live cancer. If there's a lower density, it's become a sack of water, then even if it gets very big, it's a PR by Choi. Now, we don't know that density change is going to happen in the standard of care, but if it does, and there is an increase, then it's a PR for the standard of care as well. I mean, it's the same criteria, and it is used in sarcoma. Remember, it's only for progressive disease. It is not the endpoint. The endpoint is overall survival, but it is used in both arms.

Charles Wallace: Great. That's very helpful. I guess final question from me. You mentioned the new CRO initiated in the third, or you paid in the third quarter. Does this cover both of the two studies, and does this kind of affect any timelines? Maybe just a little color on why you switched CROs.

Lewis Bender: The new CROs are only for the INVINCIBLE-3, because that's the sarcoma study. We decided to fractionate to different groups to help handle different things. So, we have this CRO that's going to be doing the reads rather than the sites. We have the CRO for statistics. We have the CRO for monitoring. We just felt that it would be better to manage it that way than what we were doing before. For the French and Swiss sites, it's the same group. It's Swiss Cancer Institute in Switzerland. It's the same group, UNICANCER in France. So, that study is separate on the CRO side from the sarcoma study.

Charles Wallace: Great. Then maybe final question from me. So, for the INVINCIBLE-4 study, you mentioned that you expect to complete enrollment by the end of 2027. Does this include any activation of U.S. sites?

Lewis Bender: It does not. It is solely right now going to be in France and Switzerland. That could change, but right now, that is, we believe, unnecessary.

Charles Wallace: Great. Thank you so much for taking my questions.

Lewis Bender: Thanks. Thanks very much, Sean.

Operator: Your next question will come from Ilya Zubkov with Freedom Broker. Please go ahead.

Ilya Zubkov: Good morning, and thank you for taking my questions. First, on INVINCIBLE-4, as the study is a part of phase II/III program, and assuming the amended regimen pCR holds up, could you elaborate on what would the registrational study look like, and roughly what would it cost?

Lewis Bender: Yes. What would a registrational study look like? So, obviously, what we're looking at here is an improvement in pCR, but also because of what we're seeing with regard to the safety, certainly with the immune-related adverse events, what we would do is we would take that data back, analyze how much better, if at all, we're seeing in terms of safety, systemic safety, less grade 3 adverse events, less immune-related adverse events. We'd go to FDA with a trial design sized based on this study for a direct comparison of our drug to the standard of care.

That study cost, obviously, if we're looking for an accelerated approval endpoint, would be costed based on the size of the pCR data. We'll have to run that through FDA. Now, we will have to do event-free survival, which will be a larger study. But the question is, will FDA, if we do see the kind of overall safety in terms of reduced grade 3 systemic adverse events and much fewer immune-related adverse events, and our pCR data is, I'm not going to expect it to be 30% better, but it could be a good 10%-15% or 20% better.

How is the combination of better safety and a pCR, if it's even smaller than what I just said, suitable to the FDA? I think before we really get into any sizing and cost, we have to have the data from this phase II study, or at least close to the data on this phase II study, and then go back to FDA with a discussion on what the appropriate study would be for approval.

Ilya Zubkov: Mm-hmm. Great. Thank you. One more question on the cash spending. I see that cash used in operations was about $2.5 million in Q3, against your $1 million per month second half guidance. What does steady state monthly burn look like for Q4 and 2027 with later sites INVINCIBLE-3 and INVINCIBLE-4, and the new manufacturing batch?

Joseph Talamo: Ilya, so we completed, you're right, about $2.7 million in operating cash burned in the third quarter. We're providing guidance of the same $1 million per month in the fourth quarter, as we exit 2026. The 2027 guidance is going to be largely dependent on bringing in additional capital and how much more we can ramp up enrollment. So, we'll provide what 2027 looks like, but you can get a feel for where we are right now at the current operations, running about $1 million a month. But again, we'll provide better guidance as we head into 2027, once we know what our capital situation looks like.

Operator: Again, if you have a question, please press star, then one. Your next question will come from James Molloy with Alliance Global Partners. Please go ahead.

James Molloy: Hey, guys. Thank you very much for taking my questions. You guys touched on quite a bit the capital issues, and that has certainly been a capital constraint, as everyone's problem, not just yours, of course. Can you talk a little bit about potential out-licensing or partnership opportunities that could offload some of the cash needs to a larger pharma partner?

Lewis Bender: Yes. That would be a key objective for us to achieve, that a partner would come in, fund part or all of the programs, and take a license to it. And those are the kinds of objectives and discussions we have. Sometimes partners want to see for themselves how it works in combination with their drug, and may fund some of those kinds of things. So, there's a lot of discussions and a lot of options on the table for the companies with whom we are in discussion.

But again, it's still a getting-to-know-you type of stage here, where they like the programs, but also potentially will have complementary products that they would want to partner with us to test our drug with their product. So, there's a lot of diverse ideas being discussed between us and some of the parties that we've been talking to.

James Molloy: Thank you for that. Is there any way to give color for us? I was looking in on sort of the number of companies or the size of the companies, or any potential ties or something that could potentially happen in 2027?

Lewis Bender: There are several large multinationals and a number of regional players as well, smaller ones. It is very early in terms of the getting to know you, but we are very pleased with the interest that we have gotten so far.

James Molloy: Yeah. Then I think, was it INVINCIBLE-3 where you mentioned you changed from just the sizing to the density to account for false progression? False progression is certainly not unheard of in immune therapies. What sort of drove that change, and how does that make interpreting the results more or less challenging?

Lewis Bender: Well, what drove the change was the patients were the doctors were seeing on the scans the tumors becoming necrotic and cystic, and then they had to pull them off because the tumor volumes were getting better. So the patients were getting potentially derived benefit, but by protocol, because the size was increasing, they had to pull them off. Then the doctors, they wanted to keep them on, but by protocol, they were obligated to remove the patient. So, that was the primary reason. Then that is when they said, "You got to use this density measurement. We are seeing good results there." Then it was kind of fortunate that we were paused at the time.

But ultimately, this switch was recommended by the doctors.

James Molloy: Okay, great. Thank you. Thank you for taking my questions.

Lewis Bender: Okay. I am going to thank everybody for the call. I just would like to say the following. Look, I believe that to make a real difference in cancer, new and different approaches may be required, even if those approaches go against the current grain of thought. I was recently asked to write a guest column for the October 15th issue of the trade publication, Drug Delivery Leader. In that article, I discussed the long history of attempts to create intratumoral therapies. I also described the common thread for why those prior attempts have really not lived up to expectations. Simply put, the tumor microenvironment is incompatible with water-based drugs.

Water-based drugs must be dosed to patients, and we have made a 100% water-based cancer-killing immune-activating product that is highly compatible with a high-fat, high-pressurized tumor microenvironment. Our phase III INVINCIBLE trial will hopefully show for the first time that a local drug, an intratumoral drug alone, can increase survival in metastatic cancer with fewer side effects. We also hope to achieve improved safety and efficacy for presurgical breast cancer patients with our drug when combined with current treatment. If our trials in sarcoma and triple-negative breast cancer are successful, I believe that this will be a transformational change for cancer patients. I want to thank everybody again for your time today.

Operator: Conference is now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. #3250. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3249. Report: Apple and Samsung outperform rivals as smartphone chip shipments tumble 21%

According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details.

At this point, most 9to5Mac readers are probably familiar with the challenges that smartphone vendors have been facing due to rising memory costs, and how Apple has managed to weather the impact better than many of its competitors.

Over the past few months, many reports have noted that while most smartphone vendors raised prices more than once throughout the year, Apple held off on increasing iPhone prices until September, with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series.

Those same reports have been showing the iPhone outperforming the broader market in smartphone, even as the industry experiences a sharp downturn.

That said, Counterpoint Research recently published a report (via MacMagazine) examining how rising memory costs and slowing smartphone demand have affected the global smartphone chip market.

According to the report, Apple remained in third place among smartphone chip vendors in the third quarter, with its market share increasing from 17% in Q3 2025 to 21%.

MediaTek still led the global smartphone SoC market with a 28% share (down 6 percentage points year-over-year), followed by Qualcomm with 22% (down from 25%).

After Apple, UNISOC ranked fourth with 13% (down from 14%), while Samsung remained in fifth with an 8% share, up from 6% in Q3 2025. Other manufacturers went from a 4% share to 8%.

Overall, the market saw a 21% decline year-over-year, though the report didn’t disclose how many chips were shipped during the quarter.

Commenting on the numbers, Counterpoint Research Senior Analyst Shivani Parashar said:

“We saw three notable flagship chipset launches in September 2026, based on TSMC’s 2nm process node: Apple’s A20 series, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. These launches are expected to boost premium smartphone SoC shipments in Q4 2026, although volumes are still likely to remain below Q4 2025 levels.”

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects global smartphone chip shipments to decline 20% year-over-year in 2026, followed by another 3% to 4% drop in 2027. The research firm also expects memory prices to continue rising next year.

During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, Apple described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” warning that further increases would continue to put pressure on its profit margins in the coming quarters.

To read Counterpoint’s full report, follow this link.

#3248. Zipline raises $1.5bn at $21.5bn valuation as Walmart adds 300 drone sites

Zipline’s valuation has nearly tripled since January. Uber is targeting a million drone deliveries a day with it by 2029, and Zipline plans to build more drones in the US.

A Zipline long-range drone drops a package by parachute.

Zipline has raised $1.5bn at a $21.5bn valuation, the drone delivery company announced on Thursday. Paradigm, WCM Investment Management and Layer Global led the round. Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest and Salesforce Ventures also invested.

On the same day, Walmart agreed to add 300 Zipline drone delivery sites in the US under a new multi-year deal. The two companies run 21 sites in Texas and Arkansas today, Bloomberg reported.

The valuation is almost three times the one Zipline reached in January, when it raised more than $600m. Bloomberg and Reuters put that earlier figure at $7.6bn, while The Wall Street Journal put it at $7.85bn.

Founder and chief executive Keller Cliffton told Bloomberg Television that demand had surprised both companies.

“I think both we and they have been quite startled by the level of customer demand.” Keller Cliffton, founder and CEO, Zipline

Zipline said it will use the money to expand its US manufacturing and hire more staff as it builds a nationwide drone delivery network. Its factory near San Francisco International Airport can make up to 20,000 aircraft a year, according to Bloomberg.

Uber, which partnered with Zipline in August, is targeting 1m drone deliveries a day with the company by 2029, Zipline said. Zipline made more than 1m deliveries in the Dallas-Fort Worth area this year. Its median order in October arrived 19 minutes after checkout, against 30 minutes or more for ground delivery, the company said.

A group of its longest-standing restaurant partners saw delivery sales rise 26% between March and October. Zipline orders made up 80% of that increase, according to the company.

Cliffton co-founded Zipline in 2014. It began by flying blood to hospitals in Rwanda. Its African business now generates positive cash flow, Cliffton told Bloomberg. The company says it has flown 150m commercial autonomous miles without a safety incident.

It runs two drones. A long-range aircraft drops packages by parachute, and a quieter short-range drone lowers home deliveries on a tether. In the US, Zipline flies in Texas, Arkansas and Ohio. It plans to launch in Arizona soon, Kelly Cloonan reported for The Wall Street Journal.

Cliffton told the Journal that the national build-out would be hard.

“We have experience doing that, but still, this is a different scale and it’s going to be hard.” Keller Cliffton, Zipline

Regulatory approvals and community concerns over noise and safety still stand in the way of wider drone delivery, Reuters reported. Walmart also works with Alphabet’s Wing. Amazon is growing its drone service to about 500 US locations. DoorDash is building its own drones, and Ireland’s Manna is building a US factory.
