#3230. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

Instagram is launching Edits on desktop today, bringing its free video editing app to Mac with a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts that can match those of other video editors.

Like Edits on mobile, Instagram says its desktop counterpart will receive weekly updates and is asking users for feedback to help shape future improvements.

A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone. You’ve got a dozen clips going, you’re trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We’re expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.

One particularly interesting feature of the new desktop app is the ability to publish videos directly to Instagram, with support for native features such as tagging, location, and trial reels.

Instagram adds that it is expanding Edits to support “multiple aspect ratios (horizontal and vertical), with 4K watermark-free export, so you can easily share to any platform, or use Edits for personal projects.”

As for the actual editing tools, Edits for desktop makes basic operations like splitting, cutting, and trimming videos easier, while also offering a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for transitions, precise audio waveforms, and advanced color grading tools such as color wheels, curves, and log conversions.

Users can also import their own LUTs and fonts, customize keyboard shortcuts, and access Instagram’s licensed audio library.

Instagram says saved audio and text styles from the mobile app are already available on desktop. However, the ability to seamlessly edit the same project across Mac and mobile is still in development.

Instagram’s desktop Edits app also offers unlimited automatic captions with support for multiple languages, as well as hundreds of sound and video effects, all for free.

#3228. Google’s Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash makes 15-second AI videos for less

The video model is now generally available, edits clips by chat and costs 30% less.

Stills generated with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, from Google’s launch graphic.

Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, its AI video model, generally available. It makes 15-second clips, up from 10, lets users edit them over several chat turns and costs 30% less, at about $0.07 a second for 720p video.

Google has made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, the latest version of its AI video model, generally available and cut its price by 30%, the company said on Thursday. It now costs about $0.07 per second of 720p video through the Gemini API, down from $0.10 a second in June.

The model can now make clips up to 15 seconds long in one go, up from 10. Users can also edit a clip over several turns in chat, such as swapping a product or background or changing the lighting, instead of making it again from scratch. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5, unveiled in June, makes 30-second clips.

Google says faces, clothes, packaging text and brand colours now stay more consistent across camera angles, with fewer glitches and jump cuts. In Google DeepMind’s own comparisons, testers preferred 1.2 over 1.1 for visual consistency 62% of the time.

Google first showed Omni Flash at its I/O conference in May, with clips capped at 10 seconds. It says it is still working on fast sports action, quick script changes and complex physics.

Google is the only US company with a model in the top 10 of one popular AI video ranking, where Chinese models hold the other nine spots.

#3226. WhatsApp adds shareable event invites and a new Events hub

WhatsApp is rolling out an update to Events just in time for holiday get-togethers. Guests can open an invite link, see the event details, and RSVP without creating a WhatsApp account or downloading the app.

When you create an event, you can add a cover photo and share the invite link by text or email. WhatsApp also gives you the option to share a QR code.

WhatsApp says your phone number is hidden from guests you don’t know, and “guests without a WhatsApp account will only see the event address after they RSVP.”

You could already create events in WhatsApp group chats and one-on-one conversations.

With this update, WhatsApp is adding a dedicated Events section in Settings where you can create invites, manage RSVPs, and see past and upcoming events you’ve organized or been invited to.

You can also set custom reminders and give guests the option to bring a plus-one.

WhatsApp says the updated Events feature will roll out to everyone over the next few weeks.

#3225. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3224. I just tried Apple’s new iMac with M6 and this sleek all-in-one is so seamless I’m ready to ditch my Mac mini

The iMac with M6 pairs a noticeable 2nm performance leap and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity with Apple’s iconic, minimalist hardware. While a higher starting price and the lack of a height-adjustable stand hold it back from perfection, its sharp 4.5K display and seamless setup make it a worthwhile upgrade for anyone holding on to an older Apple all-in-one.

Sleek, colorful design with color-matched accessories

Big performance boost thanks to Apple’s M6 and N1 chips

Surprisingly punchy speakers and solid built-in webcam

Sharp, vibrant 4.5K Retina display (with optional nano-texture glass)

Price hike on an already premium base model

Still lacks an optional height-adjustable stand

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Apple’s new iMac with M6 might look identical to its predecessor at first glance, but it’s the extra power and improved connectivity under the hood that make this upgraded all-in-one desktop continue to stand out.

Instead of drastically altering the iMac, Apple has kept more or less the same design since 2021 when the 24-inch model first debuted. Just like with the iMac M4, you’re still getting a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage webcam, and two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports at the back depending on which configuration of the new M6 chip you choose.

Similarly to the Mac mini M6 I reviewed, Apple’s M6 chip and its N1 wireless chip are the big upgrades here. While I wish there were other changes to its design — like an optional height-adjustable stand or a larger screen size — the iMac with M6 is a reliable and powerful desktop that’s incredibly simple to set up thanks to its one-cable solution. Also, unlike Apple's Studio Display monitors, the power cable is detachable, which makes cable management a breeze.

Besides being one of the best all-in-one computers, it’s also the only one that can be configured with a matte finish thanks to Apple’s optional nano-texture glass. However, is it worth upgrading from an older Mac or ditching your existing desktop setup for something more seamless? Find out in my full Apple iMac with M6 review.

2 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

4 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet built into power adapter

Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, Magic Mouse

The iMac with M6 is an elegant desktop that’s sleek and compact enough to fit into almost any space. What truly makes it shine, though, is the added muscle from Apple's M6 chip and the upgraded connectivity of the N1 — along with the fact that it remains the only all-in-one computer you can buy with an optional matte display.

The iMac with M6 that Apple sent over for review arrived in a single large box, complete with a blue fabric handle to match the desktop’s light blue colorway. Along with the computer itself, you get everything you need to start using it right away as it comes with a Magic Keyboard and a Magic Mouse.

Besides the color-matched USB-C to USB-C cable and power adapter with an Ethernet port built in that comes with the higher tier model, I really appreciated the fact that Apple includes a microfiber cloth in the box for keeping its screen fingerprint and smudge free.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The iMac with M6’s stand comes pre-attached, so there’s nothing to put together. There’s a white .5-inch border that wraps all the way around its 24-inch display along with a larger, 2-inch chin at the bottom. On the very top of the device, there’s a 12MP webcam with microphone holes on the back.

Then on the backside of the iMac with M6, there’s a hole at the top of the stand to route its power cable through along with two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports on the left side depending on which configuration you choose.

Around the corner from the power button on the back right, there’s a 3.5mm audio jack on the edge for connecting wired headphones. When you're sitting in front of the iMac, that puts the jack on your front-left — a small detail, but I really like that the cable from my headphones didn’t get in the way when using the included Magic Mouse. Though if you’re left-handed, this could be an issue if you frequently use wired headphones.

Unlike the Mac mini M4 or Mac mini M6 I’ve used previously, I just had to plug in that single power cable and power the iMac with M6 on to get started. From there, I used the included USB-C cable to pair the keyboard and mouse and I was good to go.

Although this is the first Apple all-in-one I’ve tested, the iMac with M6 felt incredibly fast and responsive right from the get go. In fact, it was a very similar experience to how it felt to upgrade from the previous Mac mini to the new Mac mini M6 and as you might have guessed, this is all thanks to Apple’s new M6 chip.

As you can see in our benchmark testing below, the change from using a 3nm process on the M4 to a 2nm process on the M6 — though literally small — makes a huge difference in terms of performance. For instance, in our Geekbench tests, we saw almost a 1,000 point single-core increase while multi-core performance jumped more than 5,000 points.

Apple has also upgraded the SSD storage in this new iMac, resulting in significantly faster read and write speeds. For those interested in video editing on the iMac with M6, this will save you a ton of time as our Handbrake encoding test (which measures how long it takes the computer to transcode a 4K video file down to 1080p) dropped by nearly two minutes, down from 5:03 on the iMac M4 to just 3:20 on the iMac M6.

The new M6 chip isn’t the only upgrade under the hood though, as this is also the first iMac with Apple’s proprietary N1 networking chip built in. Alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, it also adds native Thread support so your iMac can act as a Thread border router and directly communicate with your smart home gear.

These are all big upgrades you’ll notice in your day-to-day experience with the iMac M6 and you can read more about them in my Mac mini M6 review. However, with one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems with Wi-Fi 7 support, I saw gigabit speeds over Wi-Fi when running a few speed tests.

I could take that even further by running an Ethernet cable from my router to the iMac with M6’s power adapter as my review unit has a 2.5 GbE port built-in. It’s worth noting that while the base model doesn’t come with one, you can pay an extra $30 for the iMac power adapter with an Ethernet jack if you prefer the reliability and added speeds you get over a wired connection.

As we saw with the iMac M4 a few years ago, Apple has made serious progress when it comes to gaming on Mac and this is even more evident with the new iMac with M6. While the base model has a 10-core GPU, the upgraded one has a 12-core GPU, but both are great for gaming if you keep your expectations in check.

Given that I previously played Control on the Mac mini with M6 on Apple’s Studio Display XDR at the office, I wanted to see how Remedy’s third-person supernatural shooter played on the iMac with M6’s 4.5K Retina display at home.

Just like before, I did have to drop the resolution down to 1440p, but the game looked crisp and ran smoothly on Apple’s M6 chip. If you don’t mind sacrificing even more resolution, scaling down to 1080p gives you an even bigger performance boost across a wide variety of titles compared to the M4 chip.

In the time since I tested the Mac mini with M6, I picked up Stray on sale specifically to see how it runs on macOS. After booting up the game and playing through the intro, I’d say the iMac with M6 handled it surprisingly well.

While these are both somewhat newer titles, if you have a large backlog of Steam games you haven’t gotten around to finishing yet, the iMac with M6 could be the perfect way to play them. Even with the in-game resolution turned down, its display looks fantastic and the six-speaker system — with two pairs of force-cancelling woofers and two high-performance tweeters — helps bring the action to life too.

When the iMac with M6 was first revealed and I found out that Apple wasn’t going to bump up its screen size from 24 inches to 27 or even 32 inches, I was slightly disappointed. With the release of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, I think we might finally see a screen size bump to accommodate touch support in the next iMac — but that will be at least a few years away.

Now back to the iMac with M6, though I was initially disappointed it still had a smaller, 24-inch screen, it ended up taking me completely by surprise. Given that I do most of my work in a web browser with two side-by-side Chrome windows (each with dozens of tabs open simultaneously), I thought I wouldn’t be able to multitask the way I’m used to on the iMac with M6. Thanks to its higher 4.5K resolution though, I had more than enough screen real estate to do so quite easily.

The iMac with M6 is also slightly brighter than the older M4 variant based on our display tests. Colors are vibrant and both pictures and video appear very sharp too. I had no trouble at all editing photos in GIMP and all of my pics were color accurate on its display as well.

Since the iMac with M6’s speakers are so punchy, I decided to test its display further by watching The Wild Robot and a bit of Godzilla vs. Kong. In DreamWorks’ animated film, the robot Roz’s metallic body looked clean and crisp while Brightbill’s yellow feathers and the rest of the island’s foliage really popped.

Now if you’re partial to matte displays like I am and can’t stand seeing glare on a glossy screen, the iMac is the only all-in-one with this option available. This upgrade will set you back an extra $200 — but if you plan on using the iMac with M6 in a room with a lot of ambient light or near a window, it’s absolutely worth it.

Even though its design remains unchanged, the iMac with M6 packs in enough extra power to make it a worthwhile upgrade, especially from an older iMac with an M1 or M2 chip. Still, it does have its downsides — including a fixed-height stand that still can't be adjusted and a higher starting price over the previous model.

Let’s face it, there’s no computer or all-in-one that looks as good and features a design as iconic as Apple’s iMac. However, looks aren’t everything — and this is especially true coming from someone who also reviews home office furniture for a living.

Although you can tilt the display about 5 degrees forward or 25 degrees back, when it comes to ergonomics, this isn’t ideal. Instead, just like on Apple’s Studio Display, I’d love to see an optional height-adjustable stand for the iMac M6 too.

Sure, you can easily use a desk shelf or monitor stand to rectify this issue, but one of the main reasons someone buys an iMac over another all-in-one or a Mac mini is for the aesthetics. As I’m using one of the best standing desks from Uplift Desk for my Mac mini M6 setup, I was able to raise the desk itself to get the screen at a more ergonomic height. However, doing so makes typing on the included Magic Keyboard worse, since my forearms were tilted up instead of resting straight.

There’s something about seeing the color-matched accessories and stand together on a completely clutter-free desk that’s just really striking with an iMac. Having to ruin that look with an extra stand — or buy another accessory just to fix basic neck strain — stings even more when you take into account the other big downside with the iMac M6.

With its gorgeous display and simple setup, Apple’s iMac has always made an excellent family computer. You could set one up in a home office or even out in the living room and the entire household could use it for checking emails, managing calendars, watching videos, browsing the web or even playing games.

Thanks to RAMageddon though, the iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 — which puts a big dent in any family’s budget. Similar to the Mac mini M6, this new iMac is $200 more than its predecessor, and that’s without factoring in the additional cost of extra memory and storage. Upgrading from the base model’s 16GB of unified memory up to 24GB is an extra $200, and it’s the same story when you go from 256GB to 512GB of storage.

Add in the power adapter with Ethernet, a Magic Trackpad instead of a mouse, and a Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, and the iMac becomes a premium purchase quite quickly. Granted, it’s a machine you will be able to use for years to come with its appliance-like reliability — but still, foregoing yet another price hike would have been nice for the iMac with M6.

The iMac with M6 remains the sleekest and easiest-to-set-up all-in-one desktop you can get. There’s no other Mac or Windows machine like it, and if you want a computer that looks as good as it performs, you won’t be disappointed. The new M6 chip and the inclusion of the N1 chip give the iMac M6 a significant power and connectivity boost that make it an easy upgrade to recommend for anyone holding on to an older iMac.

Even then, I would have liked to see some tweaks to its now five-year-old design — like a larger screen or, more practically, the option to configure it with a height-adjustable stand. Still, if you don’t want to fuss with an external monitor, webcam, and loose cables, and just want a machine that works straight out of the box, the iMac with M6 is an iterative but worthwhile upgrade.

#3223. Anthropic lets Claude read your bank accounts, but not move money

The read-only Personal Finance beta links US accounts through Plaid, with no ads or financial products.

Claude’s Personal Finance beta in the mobile app.

Users link accounts through Plaid, so Claude never sees their bank password. Claude can then explain where their money went each month and spot duplicate charges or fees. It can also build charts and dashboards from balances and up to two years of transactions.

Anthropic says Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it does not offer credit cards, loans or savings accounts of its own. Hub chats are not used for training, and chats using linked accounts stay out of Claude’s shared memory, its help pages say. Anthropic also warns that Claude can make mistakes and tells users to check important figures with their bank.

There are limits. For investment, loan and card accounts, Claude reads only balances and credit limits, and users can link up to 16 US banks, according to Anthropic’s help pages. Figures already shared stay in chats, artifacts and shared links until users delete them, even after a bank is unlinked.

OpenAI launched a similar feature in May, letting ChatGPT see bank accounts through Plaid, first for its $200-a-month Pro tier. Unlike Anthropic, OpenAI has started showing ads in ChatGPT.

Anthropic calls Personal Finance “a first step.” It is exploring how Claude could work with licensed professionals and regulated firms on bigger money decisions, and has already built a version for financial advisers. It has also brought small business finances into Claude through Xero.

#3222. Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models [U: Now available]

Apple Creator Studio updates were announced late last month, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models.

At the time, Apple didn’t give a specific availability date beyond sometime in November, but the updates are rolling out today …

Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro.

Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library.

Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language.

Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates.

The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro.

Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow.

Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence.

A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.

In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge.

New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.
